```
\title{Trust Between Logical Inductors} 
\date{}
\maketitle
Consider a logical inductor $H = (H_1, H_2,\ldots)$ that represents the base human collective reasoning process. $H$ is defined over language $\mathcal{L}$ with sentence set $\mathcal{S}$, theory $\Gamma$, and $\Gamma$-complete deductive process $D_H$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in the complexity class $\mathcal{C}_H$. Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function $F: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$, and assume $F(n)>n+1$ for all $n$. Fix an effective enumeration $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)},\ldots$ of the sentences of $\mathcal{S}$. Since the enumeration can be freely chosen, take $P^{(0)}, P^{(1)}, \ldots$ to be the sequence of propositions of interest. Tying contract $n$ to $P^{(n)}$ therefore loses no generality, as any efficiently computable sequence of propositions can be studied by enumerating it in this way.

For each pair $(n,k)$ with $n\geq 1,\ 1\leq k\leq n$, define a new propositional ``threshold" symbol $\theta_{n,k}$ which should be informally read as ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $\frac{k}{n}$." Define a new language $\mathcal{L}^+$ that extends $\mathcal{L}$ with all the $\theta$ symbols, and define $\mathcal{S}^+$ to be the sentence set over $\mathcal{L}^+$. 

Define a schema $\{\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}: n\geq 1,\ 2\leq k\leq n\}$ of ``monotonicity" axioms. Each axiom informally says that ``clearing the $\frac{k}{n}$ threshold implies clearing the $\frac{k-1}{n}$ threshold." 

A world for $\mathcal{L}^+$ is a truth assignment $W:\mathcal{S}^+\to \{0,1\}$. For $W$ propositionally consistent with the monotonicity axioms, define the value of contract $n$ in $W$ by \[\text{val}_W(n) := \frac{\#\{k: 1\leq k\leq n,\ W(\theta_{n,k})=1\}}{n}\]
Due to the monotonicity axioms, the set of indices that appears in the numerator must be an initial segment $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for some $0\leq m \leq n$, so we also have $\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m}{n}$. 

The following simultaneously defines a coupled pair $A$ that represents an AI reasoner and $H^+$ that represents the human reasoner augmented with the ability to observe published quotes of $A$'s outputs. These two mutually referential inductors are defined by recursion on time. Two timing delays ensure this recursion's well-foundedness: $H^+$ receives the quotes from $A$ one time step after they are posted, and $A$'s contracts settle only at a time step greater than $F(n)$, after which the referenced future price $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ already exists.

Let $\mathcal{C}_A$ be a complexity class with $\mathcal{C}_H \subseteq \mathcal{C}_A$ such that, in the coupled construction below, the map $n \mapsto H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. $\mathcal{C}_A$ must also satisfy the "polynomial overhead" condition: If a function $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, then so too is any function that, on input $n$, makes at most $\text{poly}(n)$ calls to $g$ and performs at most $\text{poly}(n)$ additional elementary steps. Concretely, computing $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ means simulating the coupled system to depth $F(n)$. Writing $R(t)$ for the per-day runtime of the logical-inductor implementation for $H^+$ (left open in Garrabrant et al.\ \S5.5), the assumption is that $\mathcal{C}_A$ contains $n \mapsto R(F(n))$. Under the further hypothesis that $R(t) = \mathrm{poly}(t)$, two example instantiations are $\mathcal{C}_H = \mathrm{P}$, $\mathcal{C}_A = \mathrm{P}$, $F(n)=n^2$ and $\mathcal{C}_H = \mathrm{P}$,  $\mathcal{C}_A = \mathrm{EXP}$, $F(n)=2^n$.

Let the ``settlement-time" function $\sigma: \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ be a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable function such that $\sigma(n) > F(n)$ and also that $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ can be computed within $\sigma(n)$ steps.

Define a deductive process $D_A$ as follows. At each time $t$, $D_A^t$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item The monotonicity axioms $\theta_{n,k}\rightarrow \theta_{n,k-1}$ for $n\leq t$ and $2\leq k \leq n$
  \item For each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\leq t$, let $m_{n}^*$ be defined as the integer $m$ with $0\leq m \leq n$ that minimizes the value of $\left|\frac{m}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\right|$ (with ties going to the lower integer). Then $D_A^t$ includes $\theta_{n,k}$ for $k\leq m_{n}^*$ and $\neg \theta_{n,k}$ for $k>m_{n}^*$. 
\end{enumerate}
The second component should be understood as the settlement of contract \(n\) translated to the threshold propositions. In particular, for every \(t\geq \sigma(n)\) and every \(W\) consistent with \(D^t_A\), \(\text{val}_W(n)=\frac{m^*_{n}}{n}\), which differs from \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) by at most \(\frac{1}{2n}\). Note that since items 1 and 2 range over finitely many values, each \(D_A^t\) is finite. \(D_A\) is also computable as part of the simultaneous construction: each \(m^*_{n}\) is computable because \(\sigma(n)>F(n)\), so the value \(H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\) has already been computed by the time the settlement is inserted. Finally, note that each \(D_A^t\) is also consistent: settlements respect the monotonicity axioms, and the settlement steps for distinct \(n\) involve disjoint sets of threshold propositions. Thus, the logical induction criterion relative to \(D_A\) is well-posed.

Define $A = (A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ that satisfies the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to the deductive process $D_A$.

For each $n \geq 1$, define the contract $C_{n}$ as the affine combination $C_{n} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k}$. By linearity, $W(C_{n}) = \text{val}_W(n)$ for every world $W$ consistent with the monotonicity axioms. We write $A_t(C_{n}) := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n A_t(\theta_{n,k})$ for the price $A$ induces on the contract at time $t$; this is a rational in $[0,1]$. The contracts are affine combinations of threshold symbols already priced by $A$ rather than separate objects in $A$'s market.

Define a deductive process $D_H^+$ extending $D_H$ with two additional streams of data. In order for $H^+$ to learn the reliable calibration of $A$, it requires quotes of $A$'s prices and the settlements those quotes are eventually audited against. At each time $t$, $D_H^{+,t}$ contains all of the following:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item $D_H^t$, so that $D_H^+$ extends the original deductive process $D_H$
  \item A record of the published quotes $a_i := A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$
  \item For each $i$ with $F(i) < t$, the realized settlement of contract $i$: the threshold profile $\theta_{i,k}$ for $k \leq m_i^*$ and $\neg\theta_{i,k}$ for $k > m_i^*$
\end{enumerate}
Items 1 and 3 use the same background and settlement profiles as the corresponding components of $D_A$, though $D_H^+$ records the realized settlement once $F(i)<t$ while $D_A$ inserts the formal contract settlement at time $\sigma(i)$. Item 2 is the new content, recording $A$'s quotes after the one-step delay. As part of the simultaneous construction each $D_H^{+,t}$ is finite and computable, and is consistent: the settlement profiles of item 3 are initial segments respecting the monotonicity axioms, and the quote records of item 2 concern values disjoint from the threshold propositions.

Define $H^+$ as a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.

Write $a_n := A_n(C_n)$ for $A$'s published quote, recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, and $Y_n := H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for $H^+$'s own future price that the quote is audited against. For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, let $g_{r,s,\delta} : [0,1] \to [0,1]$ be the continuous function equal to $1$ on $[r,s]$, equal to $0$ outside $[r-\delta, s+\delta]$, and linear in between, and set $G_n := g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$. Since $a_n$ is recorded in $D_H^{+,n+1}$, both $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable by $H^+$ from time $n+1$ onward. Throughout, for real-valued sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$, $x_n \simeq_n y_n$ means $x_n - y_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, following the convention of Garrabrant et al.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:existence}
There exist sequences $A = (A_1, A_2, \ldots)$ and $H^+ = (H^+_1, H^+_2, \ldots)$, 
together with the deductive processes $D_A$ and $D_H^+$, such that: $D_A$ and 
$D_H^+$ are computable deductive processes; $A$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ 
satisfying the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$; and $H^+$ is a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the logical 
induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The four sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, $(D_H^{+,t})$ are defined 
together by a single recursion on $t$. We fix uniform computable instantiations 
of the construction of Garrabrant et al.\ \S5, one for each market, whose 
time-$t$ outputs are computed from the finite information used by the 
construction up to stage $t$. We run two such constructions, one per market, 
interleaved with the definitions of the deductive processes.

Suppose all four sequences have been defined at every stage $s < t$. We define 
the stage-$t$ objects as follows.

\emph{Deductive processes.} $D_A^t$ is given by its definition. Its only 
dependence on $H^+$ is through the settlement values $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ for 
$n$ with $\sigma(n) \leq t$; since $\sigma(n) > F(n)$, each such $n$ has 
$F(n) < \sigma(n) \leq t$, so these are prices $H^+_{F(n)}$ at times 
$F(n) < t$, already defined. Likewise $D_H^{+,t}$ depends on $A$ only through the 
quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$, again already defined. Both stage-$t$ 
deductive sets are therefore computable from stage-$(<t)$ data, and are finite 
and consistent as shown in their definitions.

\emph{Markets.} With $D_A^{\leq t}$ now in hand, the fixed construction yields 
its time-$t$ pricing $A_t$ from the finite information used by the construction 
up to stage $t$ and its own stages before $t$; similarly $H^+_t$ is produced 
from the corresponding finite information from $D_H^{+,\leq t}$. Neither 
market-step references any stage-$t$ price of the other: $A_t$ uses only the 
stage-$t$ information from $D_A$ (which depended on $H^+$ at times $< t$) and 
$(A_s)_{s<t}$, and symmetrically for $H^+_t$.

Every stage-$t$ object thus depends only on stage-$(<t)$ objects, so the 
recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$, 
$(D_H^{+,t})$ are computable; in particular $D_A$ and $D_H^+$ are computable 
deductive processes. Finally, because each market is produced by the fixed 
construction over its own (computable, consistent) deductive process, $A$ 
satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}_A$ relative to 
$D_A$, and $H^+$ satisfies it against $\mathcal{C}_H$ relative to $D_H^+$. We 
emphasize that this establishes existence and computability only; that $A$'s 
traders can compute the settlement values \emph{within $\mathcal{C}_A$} is the 
separate assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$ above, used in the Tracking Theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pinning}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values 
        $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ and a $\mathcal{C}$-computable 
        settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \simeq_n v_n.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n v_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]\label{thm:tracking}
\[
A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable; the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
since $m_n^*$ rounds $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, which is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
by the standing assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$. For hypothesis~2: by the
construction of $D_A$, for every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have $\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\
$W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since $C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is
an average of $n$ values $W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have
$W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at every $t$, independently of
consistency.

Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} yields $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n \tfrac{m_n^*}{n}$. By the construction
of $D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n}
\to 0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:vanishing}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable from the information available in $D^n$, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping and admissibility argument are 
unchanged. Since $W(X_n) \in [-B,B]$, a single open sold position opened when 
$P_i(X_i)>\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ has value
\[
\rho_i(P_i(X_i)-W(X_i)) \geq -B,
\]
and a single open bought position opened when $P_i(X_i)<-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$
has value
\[
\rho_i(W(X_i)-P_i(X_i)) \geq -B.
\]
Thus the downside from the at-most-one unsettled position is bounded below by
$-B$. The only substantive change is at settlement: a settled trigger position
opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes $\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$ in the sold
case, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have
$|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger position
($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a bought
one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and the fact
that the settled values vanish. Infinitely many settled triggers then give
plausible net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B$ along a subsequence,
unbounded above, while the downside stays $\geq -B$. This exploits $P$,
contradicting the logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:calibration}
For any bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$ and margin $\delta > 0$, with 
$G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ as above, $H^+$ comes to expect $A$'s quote to match 
the settlement on the cases $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, G_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := G_n(a_n - Y_n)$. Since $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants and $Y_n$ is 
the value of the contract $C_n$ pinned by the settlement profile, 
$Z_n = G_n a_n - G_n C_n$ is a bounded affine combination of the threshold 
sentences $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n| \leq 1$. The quote $a_n$ is recorded in 
$D_H^+$ once $n < t$ and the profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ is pinned once 
$F(n) < t$, so $Z_n$ is pinned by $D_H^+$ at $\tau(n) := F(n)+1$, which is 
$\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is. Its realized value is 
$w_n = G_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)$; by the Tracking Theorem $a_n - Y_n \to 0$, and the 
profile encodes $Y_n$ up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, so 
$|w_n| \leq |a_n - Y_n| + \tfrac{1}{2n} \to 0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:vanishing} 
requires $X_m$ to be computable from $D^m$, whereas $Z_n$ depends on $a_n$, 
which $D_H^+$ records only at time $n+1$; we therefore apply the lemma to the 
shifted sequence $\widehat Z_m := Z_{m-1}$ for $m \geq 2$, with 
$\widehat\tau(m) := F(m-1)+1$, since $a_{m-1}$ is recorded in $D_H^+$ by time $m$. 
This gives
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Z_n] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
$H^+$ comes to trust $A$. With $G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ the bin weight,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, \mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\, G_n \,\bigr] \simeq_n a_n\, G_n,
\]
equivalently, since $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants observable at time $n+1$,
\[
G_n\, H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n G_n\, a_n.
\]
Reading the weight $G_n$ as a soft conditioning on the event ``$A$ quotes near 
$[r,s]$'', this says that on the cases where $A$ quotes near $[r,s]$, $H^+$'s 
credence in $P^{(n)}$ agrees with $A$'s published quote.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The argument composes three facts: $H^+$ trusts its own future credence; $A$'s 
quote tracks that future credence; hence $H^+$ trusts $A$'s quote.

\emph{Self-trust.} The weight $G_n = g_{r,s,\delta}(a_n)$ is a continuous 
function of the quote $a_n$, recorded in $D_H^+$ by time $n+1 \leq F(n)$; hence 
$G_n$ is $H^+$-generable and lies in $[0,1]$, so it is an admissible weight for 
Theorem 4.12.3 (No Expected Net Update under Conditionals) of Garrabrant et al. 
Applying it to $H^+$ with the indicator $\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})$ and weight $G_n$, 
and using $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{F(n)}(\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})) = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) = 
Y_n$ by Theorem 4.8.6 (Expectations of Indicators),
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] 
\simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,G_n].
\]
This says $H^+$'s current credence already agrees with what it expects its own 
future self at time $F(n)$ to believe.

\emph{Quote tracks future credence.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:calibration}, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n G_n] \simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n]$, which 
swaps $H^+$'s future credence $Y_n$ for $A$'s quote $a_n$. This is the step that 
rests on Tracking: $A$ is forced by its own induction criterion to predict 
$Y_n$, so $H^+$ learns the quote and the future credence coincide.

\emph{Composition.} Since $a_n$ and $G_n$ are constants at time $n+1$, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n G_n] = a_n G_n$ and, again by Theorem 4.8.6, 
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,G_n] = G_n H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$. 
Chaining the three displays gives both stated forms.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Along any subsequence on which $A$ quotes in $[r,s]$ with non-vanishing 
frequency,
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n.
\]
In particular, whenever $A$ quotes within $[r,s]$, $H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ 
comes to lie in $[r,s]$ up to a vanishing error.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
On such a subsequence $G_n$ is bounded below by some $\gamma > 0$, so dividing 
the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:forcedtrust} through by $G_n$ gives 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n$. When $a_n \in [r,s]$ we have $G_n = 1$, so 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$ lies in $[r,s]$ up to an additive error vanishing in $n$.
\end{proof}

\bigskip

The following is a general property of logical inductors, independent of the 
coupled construction.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:projection}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over a language $\mathcal{L} = 
\mathcal{L}_0 \cup \{p\}$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against a 
complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a 
computable deductive process $D$ in which the atom $p$ does not occur. For an 
$\mathcal{L}$-sentence $\chi$, write $\chi^\top$ and $\chi^\bot$ for the $p$-free 
sentences obtained by substituting a fixed tautology, respectively its negation, 
for every occurrence of $p$ in $\chi$. For $c \in (0,1) \cap \mathbb{Q}$ define 
the market $P^c$ over $\mathcal{L}$ by
\[
P^c_n(\chi) := c\,P_n(\chi^\top) + (1-c)\,P_n(\chi^\bot).
\]
Then $P^c$ satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}$ 
relative to $D$, agrees with $P$ on every $p$-free sentence, and 
$P^c_\infty(p) = c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A trade on day $i$ is an affine combination of sentences; write $T_i[\phi]$ for 
its coefficient on $\phi$ (shares bought, negative for sold), so that the trade 
costs $\sum_\phi T_i[\phi]\,P^c_i(\phi)$ at the prevailing prices and pays 
$\sum_\phi T_i[\phi]\,W(\phi)$ in a world $W$.

Because $p$ does not occur in $D$, at every time $t$ the plausible worlds factor 
over the truth value of $p$: writing $\mathrm{PC}_0(D^t)$ for the assignments to 
$p$-free sentences propositionally consistent with $D^t$, every 
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ has the form $(W_0, b)$ with $W_0 \in \mathrm{PC}_0(D^t)$ 
and $b = W(p) \in \{0,1\}$, and \emph{both} extensions $(W_0, 0)$ and 
$(W_0, 1)$ lie in $\mathrm{PC}(D^t)$. By the Shannon expansion 
$\chi \equiv (p \wedge \chi^\top) \vee (\neg p \wedge \chi^\bot)$,
\[
W(\chi) = b\,W_0(\chi^\top) + (1-b)\,W_0(\chi^\bot).
\]

Suppose toward contradiction that a trader $T \in \mathcal{C}$ exploits $P^c$. 
Its holdings after day $n$, valued in a world $(W_0, b)$, are
\[
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, b) = \sum_{i \le n} \sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(W(\phi) - P^c_i(\phi)\bigr).
\]
Define traders $T^\top$ and $T^\bot$ \emph{against $P$} that on each day $i$ 
trade the $p$-free sentences $\phi^\top$, respectively $\phi^\bot$, with the same 
coefficients $T_i[\phi]$ at $P$'s prevailing prices. Since each $P^c_i$ is an 
affine --- hence continuous --- function of the prices of $P$, the coefficients 
$T_i[\phi]$, which are continuous expressible features of the history of $P^c$, 
are continuous expressible features of the history of $P$ of the same rank; the 
substitutions $\phi \mapsto \phi^\top, \phi^\bot$ are computable; and each day 
trades $\operatorname{poly}(i)$ sentences. By closure under polynomial overhead, 
$T^\top, T^\bot \in \mathcal{C}$. Write
\[
V^\top_n(W_0) := W_0\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n} T^\top_i\Bigr) = \sum_{i\le n}\sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(W_0(\phi^\top) - P_i(\phi^\top)\bigr),
\]
and $V^\bot_n(W_0)$ analogously.

Substituting $P^c_i(\phi) = c\,P_i(\phi^\top) + (1-c)P_i(\phi^\bot)$ and 
$W(\phi) = b\,W_0(\phi^\top) + (1-b)W_0(\phi^\bot)$, and adding and subtracting 
$P_i(\phi^\top)$ in the case $b=1$ and $P_i(\phi^\bot)$ in the case $b=0$,
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 1) &= V^\top_n(W_0) + (1-c)\,\Delta_n,\\
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 0) &= V^\bot_n(W_0) - c\,\Delta_n,
\end{align*}
where $\Delta_n := \sum_{i\le n}\sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(P_i(\phi^\top) - P_i(\phi^\bot)\bigr)$ is independent of the 
world. The $c$-weighted combination therefore cancels $\Delta_n$:
\[
c\,\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 1) + (1-c)\,\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 0) 
= c\,V^\top_n(W_0) + (1-c)V^\bot_n(W_0) = W_0\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i\Bigr),
\]
where $\widehat T := c\,T^\top + (1-c)\,T^\bot$ is a single trader against $P$, 
and $\widehat T \in \mathcal{C}$.

Now invoke the assumed exploitation. \emph{Bounded below:} there is $B$ with 
$\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, b) \ge -B$ for all $n$ and all $(W_0, b) \in 
\mathrm{PC}(D^n)$. Since both $(W_0, 0)$ and $(W_0, 1)$ are plausible for every 
plausible $W_0$, the displayed identity gives 
$W_0(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i) \ge -B$ for all $n$ and $W_0$, so the $P$-trader 
$\widehat T$ is bounded below. As $P$ is a logical inductor, $\widehat T$ does 
not exploit it, hence it is also bounded above: 
$W_0(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i) \le B'$ for some $B'$ and all $n, W_0$. 
\emph{Unbounded above:} along some $n_k \to \infty$ there are plausible 
$(W_0^{(k)}, b_k)$ with $\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, b_k) \to +\infty$; pass to 
a subsequence on which $b_k$ is constant, say $b_k = 1$ (the case $b_k = 0$ is 
symmetric, exchanging the roles of $c$ and $1-c$). Then 
$\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) \to +\infty$, and
\[
(1-c)\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 0) 
= W_0^{(k)}\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n_k}\widehat T_i\Bigr) 
- c\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) 
\le B' - c\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) \to -\infty.
\]
As $c < 1$, $\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 0) \to -\infty$, contradicting the 
lower bound $-B$ at the plausible worlds $(W_0^{(k)}, 0)$. Hence no 
$T \in \mathcal{C}$ exploits $P^c$, so $P^c$ satisfies the logical induction 
criterion relative to $D$.

Finally, for $p$-free $\chi$ we have $\chi^\top = \chi^\bot = \chi$, so 
$P^c_n(\chi) = P_n(\chi)$; and $P^c_n(p) = c\,P_n(\top) + (1-c)P_n(\bot) \to c$ 
since $P_n(\top) \to 1$ and $P_n(\bot) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:noncategoricity}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection}, for every $c \in (0,1) \cap 
\mathbb{Q}$ there is a logical inductor over $D$ against $\mathcal{C}$ whose 
limiting credence in $p$ equals $c$ and which agrees with $P$ on every $p$-free 
sentence. In particular, two logical inductors over the same $D$ and the same 
$\mathcal{C}$ can agree on every $p$-free sentence yet assign limiting credences 
$c \neq c'$ to $p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} to obtain $P^c$ and $P^{c'}$; each agrees with 
$P$ off $p$, and $P^c_\infty(p) = c$, $P^{c'}_\infty(p) = c'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If the proposition of interest $P^{(n)}$ is decided by $\Gamma$, then
\[
H_\infty(P^{(n)}) = H^+_\infty(P^{(n)}) = \mathbf{1}[\Gamma \vdash P^{(n)}].
\]
\item Provided $\mathcal{L}$ has a propositional atom occurring in neither 
$\Gamma$ nor $D_H$, the augmented and base limits need not agree: there exist 
such an atom $\phi$, taken as the proposition of interest, and an admissible 
coupled system $(A, H^+)$ --- computable $D_A, D_H^+$ with $A$ a logical inductor 
over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$ and $H^+$ a logical inductor over $D_H^+$ 
against $\mathcal{C}_H$, built from the same $\Gamma$, $D_H$, $\mathcal{C}_H$, 
$\mathcal{C}_A$, $F$, $\sigma$ and satisfying the Tracking and Forced Trust 
theorems --- with
\[
H^+_\infty(\phi) \neq H_\infty(\phi).
\]
Indeed, with $c_0 := H_\infty(\phi) \in (0,1)$ fixed (Theorem 4.6.2, 
Non-Dogmatism, of Garrabrant et al.), every $c \in (0,1) \cap \mathbb{Q}$ is 
realized as $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ by some such system.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) The process $D_H$ is $\Gamma$-complete, and $D_H^+ \supseteq D_H$ is 
$\Gamma$-complete as well; by Theorem 4.2.1 (Provability Induction) of Garrabrant 
et al.\ a logical inductor over a $\Gamma$-complete process assigns limiting 
credence $1$ to $\Gamma$-provable sentences and $0$ to $\Gamma$-refutable ones. 
Hence $H_\infty(\phi)$ and $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ both equal $\mathbf{1}[\Gamma 
\vdash \phi]$.

(ii) Fix such an atom $\phi$ and take it as the proposition of interest, 
$P^{(n)} = \phi$ for all $n$. Run the simultaneous recursion of 
Lemma~\ref{lem:existence}, producing markets $B_A$ over $D_A$ and $B_H$ over 
$D_H^+$ from the fixed \S5 construction, but project each market step: in the 
notation of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection}, with the atom there taken to be $\phi$, 
set $A_t := (B_A)^c_t$ and $H^+_t := (B_H)^c_t$, and use these projected prices 
wherever the construction refers to the markets --- in particular, $D_A$ settles 
contract $n$ using $H^+_{F(n)}(\phi) = (B_H)^c_{F(n)}(\phi)$.

The projection is a computable post-processing of a single market step, so the 
recursion remains well-founded under the same two delays: $D_A^t$ uses 
$H^+_{F(n)}$ only for $\sigma(n) \le t$, hence at times $F(n) < t$, and 
$D_H^{+,t}$ uses the quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$. Because each contract 
$C_n$ is built from threshold symbols, $A_i(C_i) = (B_A)^c_i(C_i) = (B_A)_i(C_i)$, 
so the recorded quotes, and hence $D_H^+$ itself, are exactly those of the base 
construction. All three deductive processes are free of $\phi$, so 
Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} applies to each market: $A = (B_A)^c$ is a logical 
inductor over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$ and $H^+ = (B_H)^c$ is a logical 
inductor over $D_H^+$ against $\mathcal{C}_H$, with $A_\infty(\phi) = 
H^+_\infty(\phi) = c$. Being genuine logical inductors over the constructed 
processes, they satisfy the hypotheses of the Tracking and Forced Trust theorems, 
which apply unchanged. For $c \neq c_0$ this gives $H^+_\infty(\phi) = c \neq c_0 
= H_\infty(\phi)$.
\end{proof}
```

## Simplified lemma (replaces `lem:calibration`)

```latex
\begin{lemma}[Quote tracking]\label{lem:calibration}
With $a_n = A_n(C_n)$ and $Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ as above, $H^+$ comes to
expect $A$'s quote to coincide with the settled value of the contract it audits:
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, a_n - Y_n \,\bigr] \simeq_n 0,
\]
equivalently, since $a_n$ is observable at time $n+1$,
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n] \simeq_n a_n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := a_n - C_n$. Since $a_n$ is a constant recorded in $D_H^+$ from time
$n+1$ and $Y_n$ is the value of the contract $C_n$ pinned by the settlement
profile, $Z_n$ is a bounded affine combination of the threshold sentences
$\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n| \leq 1$. The profile $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ is pinned
once $F(n) < t$, so $Z_n$ is pinned by $D_H^+$ at $\tau(n) := F(n)+1$, which is
$\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is. Its realized value is $w_n = a_n - m_n^*/n$;
by the Tracking Theorem $a_n - Y_n \to 0$, and the profile encodes $Y_n$ up to
$\tfrac{1}{2n}$, so $|w_n| \leq |a_n - Y_n| + \tfrac{1}{2n} \to 0$. Because $a_n$
is recorded only at time $n+1$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:vanishing} to the shifted
sequence $\widehat Z_m := Z_{m-1}$ ($m \geq 2$) with
$\widehat\tau(m) := F(m-1)+1$, computable from $D_H^{+,m}$ since $a_{m-1}$ is
recorded by time $m$. This gives
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n - Y_n] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n) \simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}
```

## Cleaner Theorem 2 (replaces `thm:forcedtrust`)

```latex
\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
$H^+$ comes to trust $A$: it sets its credence in $P^{(n)}$ to $A$'s published
quote,
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n.
\]
This is the No-Expected-Net-Update law (Theorem 4.12.2 of Garrabrant et al.) with
$A$'s quote $a_n$ in the place of $H^+$'s own future credence: on seeing the quote
$a_n$, $H^+$ updates its credence in $P^{(n)}$ to $a_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The argument composes three facts, exactly as for self-trust, with $A$'s quote
substituted for $H^+$'s future self.

\emph{Self-trust.} Since $F$ is a strictly increasing deferral function with
$F(n) > n+1$, the shifted map $m \mapsto F(m-1)$ is again a deferral function, as
$F(m-1) > m$. Applying No Expected Net Update (Theorem 4.12.2) to $H^+$ along this
deferral, with the sentence $P^{(n)}$ evaluated at time $n+1$,
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\,H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\,\bigr]
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n].
\]
$H^+$'s current credence already equals what it expects its time-$F(n)$ self to
believe.

\emph{Quote tracks future credence.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:calibration},
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n] \simeq_n a_n$. This is the step that rests on
Tracking: $A$ is forced by its own induction criterion to predict $Y_n$, so $H^+$,
auditing the quote against the settled contract, comes to expect the quote and its
own future credence to coincide.

\emph{Composition.} Chaining the two displays,
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n] \simeq_n a_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Whenever $A$ quotes within a bin $[r,s] \subseteq [0,1]$, $H^+$'s credence in
$P^{(n)}$ comes to lie in $[r,s]$ up to a vanishing error: if $a_n \in [r,s]$ then
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \in [r,s]$ up to an additive error vanishing in $n$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from $H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n$.
\end{proof}
```

## Calibration lemma (weighted, replaces `lem:calibration`)

```latex
\begin{lemma}[Quote tracking]\label{lem:calibration}
Let $w_n \in [0,1]$ be any $H^+$-generable weight observable at time $n+1$
(e.g.\ any continuous function of the recorded quote $a_n$). Then
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, w_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := w_n a_n - w_n C_n$. Since $w_n$ and $a_n$ are constants observable at
$n+1$ and $Y_n$ is the value of the contract $C_n$ pinned by the settlement
profile, $Z_n$ is a bounded affine combination of the threshold sentences
$\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n|\leq 1$, pinned by $D_H^+$ at $\tau(n):=F(n)+1$
($\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is). Its realized value is
$w_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)$; by Tracking $a_n - Y_n \to 0$ and the profile encodes $Y_n$
up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, so $|w_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)| \leq |a_n-Y_n|+\tfrac{1}{2n}\to 0$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:vanishing} to the shift $\widehat Z_m := Z_{m-1}$ with
$\widehat\tau(m):=F(m-1)+1$ (so $a_{m-1}$ is recorded by time $m$) gives
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[w_n(a_n-Y_n)] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n)\simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}
```

This is your original lemma with $G_n$ renamed $w_n$; nothing else changes.

## Theorem 2 in 4.12.4 form (replaces `thm:forcedtrust`)

```latex
\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
Let $\delta_n$ be an e.c.\ sequence of positive rationals and $p_n$ an
$H^+$-generable sequence of rational probabilities. Writing
$w_n := \mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(a_n > p_n)$ for the soft indicator that $A$ quotes
$P^{(n)}$ above $p_n$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, \mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\, w_n \,\bigr]
\;\succsim_n\;
p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\,w_n\,].
\]
That is: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ with probability at least $p_n$,
$H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ is at least $p_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The weight $w_n$ is $H^+$-generable, lies in $[0,1]$, and is a constant from time
$n+1$ on; it is therefore an admissible conditioning weight for Theorem 4.12.3
(No Expected Net Update under Conditionals) of Garrabrant et al.

\emph{Self-trust.} Applying Theorem 4.12.3 to $H^+$ with the indicator
$\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})$, weight $w_n$, and deferral $m\mapsto F(m-1)$ (a deferral
function since $F(n)>n+1$), and using
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{F(n)}(\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)}))=Y_n$ (Theorem 4.8.6),
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,w_n]
\simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,w_n].
\]
(Because $w_n$ is already settled at $n+1$, this conditional self-trust step in
fact collapses to ordinary self-trust, Theorem 4.12.2 --- the one point at which
our setting is simpler than 4.12.4, whose conditioning event lies in the future.)

\emph{Quote tracks future credence.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:calibration},
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n w_n] \simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n w_n] = a_n w_n$,
swapping $H^+$'s future credence $Y_n$ for $A$'s quote $a_n$; this is the step
that rests on Tracking.

\emph{No false positives.} By Definition 4.3.2, $w_n>0$ forces $a_n>p_n$, so
$a_n w_n \geq p_n w_n$ pointwise (with equality when $w_n=0$). Hence
$a_n w_n \geq p_n w_n = p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[w_n]$, and chaining the three
displays gives the claim.
\end{proof}
```

(Define `\succsim_n` as Garrabrant's "≥ up to vanishing error": $x_n \succsim_n y_n$ iff $x_n \ge y_n - o(1)$ — their `&`.)

## Why it reads as 4.12.4

The correspondence is exact, slot for slot:

| | conditioning event | conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| **4.12.4 (Self-Trust)** | $H^+$'s own future credence $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) > p_n$ | credence now $\succsim p_n$ |
| **Forced Trust** | $A$'s published quote $a_n > p_n$ | credence now $\succsim p_n$ |

Garrabrant's gloss of 4.12.4 — "if you ask what it believes about $\varphi$ now, given that it's going to believe $\varphi$ with probability $\ge p$ later, it answers $\ge p$" — becomes, verbatim, "if you ask $H^+$ what it believes about $P^{(n)}$ now, given that $A$ quotes it at $\ge p$, it answers $\ge p$." Forced Trust *is* 4.12.4 with $A$'s quote substituted for the future self, and Tracking is what licenses the substitution. That framing has the side benefit of making the self-trust-through-proxy structure from the last turn legible on the face of the theorem rather than buried: the only thing that changed between the two rows is whose assertion fills the conditioning slot.

The soft indicator $\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}$ is doing the same job here as in 4.12.4 — it's the device that avoids the degenerate hard-conditional behavior (the $\mathbf{1}(\varphi_n)\wedge(\cdots)$ pathology Garrabrant flags right after 4.12.4), so you'll want the same one-sentence remark about why the threshold is continuous. The symmetric lower statement ($a_n < p_n \Rightarrow$ credence $\precsim p_n$) holds by the identical argument with $\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(a_n < p_n)$, if you want both halves.

So you can write it in exact 4.12.2 form, keep the expectation visible to make the parallel land, and note the collapse:

```latex
\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \;\simeq_n\; \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl(``A_n(C_n)"\bigr).
\]
Since $A_n(C_n)$ is recorded in $D_H^+$ as the constant $a_n$ by time $n+1$, the
right-hand side equals $a_n$, so equivalently $H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n$:
$H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ matches $A$'s published quote.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Self-trust.} Since $F$ is a strictly increasing deferral function with
$F(n)>n+1$, the shift $m\mapsto F(m-1)$ is again a deferral function. No Expected
Net Update (Theorem 4.12.2 of Garrabrant et al.), applied to $H^+$ along this
deferral with the sentence $P^{(n)}$ at time $n+1$, gives
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \;\simeq_n\; \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl(``H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})"\bigr)
= \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n].
\]

\emph{Quote tracking.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:calibration} (with weight $\equiv 1$),
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\,a_n - Y_n\,]\simeq_n 0$, i.e.
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n] \;\simeq_n\; \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl(``A_n(C_n)"\bigr).
\]
This is the step that rests on Tracking: $A$ is forced by its own criterion to
predict $Y_n$, so $H^+$, auditing the quote against the settled contract, comes to
expect quote and future credence to coincide.

\emph{Composition.} Chaining,
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}(``A_n(C_n)")$; and
$``A_n(C_n)"$ is the recorded constant $a_n$.
\end{proof}
```

with the supporting lemma in its unweighted form:

```latex
\begin{lemma}[Quote tracking]\label{lem:calibration}
$\displaystyle \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, a_n - Y_n \,\bigr] \simeq_n 0.$
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := a_n - C_n$. As $a_n$ is a constant recorded from time $n+1$ and $Y_n$
is the value of $C_n$ pinned by the settlement profile, $Z_n$ is a bounded affine
combination of the $\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n|\le 1$, pinned by $D_H^+$ at

$|a_n - m_n^*/n|\le |a_n-Y_n| + \tfrac1{2n}\to 0$ by Tracking. Applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:vanishing} to $\widehat Z_m := Z_{m-1}$ with
$\widehat\tau(m):=F(m-1)+1$ gives $H^+_{n+1}(Z_n)\simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}
```

```latex
% Language: extend L^+ to L^{++} with quote-threshold symbols.
% For n >= 1, 1 <= k <= n, a symbol \beta_{n,k}, read
% "A's day-n quote A_n(C_n) is at least k/n", with monotonicity axioms
% \beta_{n,k} -> \beta_{n,k-1}. Define the quote-contract
\[
  \widehat C_n := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \beta_{n,k},
  \qquad W(\widehat C_n) = \frac{\#\{k : W(\beta_{n,k})=1\}}{n}.
\]
% Augment D_H^+ with a fourth stream: for each i with i < t, having
% recorded a_i, include the settled quote profile \beta_{i,k} for
% k <= \widehat m_i and \neg\beta_{i,k} for k > \widehat m_i, where
```

```latex
$\displaystyle H^+_n(\widehat C_n) \simeq_n H^+_n(C_n).$

$H^+_n(\widehat C_n - C_n)\simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}
```

```
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:existence}

construction up to stage $t$. We run two such constructions, one per market, 
interleaved with the definitions of the deductive processes.

the stage-$t$ objects as follows.

recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$,

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pinning}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
that is closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive 
process $D$. Let 
\[
X_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^{q(n)} \alpha_{n,\ell}\, \psi_{n,\ell}
\]
be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in $\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ (i.e.\ the maps $n \mapsto q(n)$, 
        $n \mapsto (\alpha_{n,\ell})_\ell$, and $n \mapsto (\psi_{n,\ell})_\ell$) 
        is $\mathcal{C}$-computable, with $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable sequence of values 
        $v_n \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1]$ and a $\mathcal{C}$-computable 
        settlement-time function $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every world 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
        \[
        W(X_n) = v_n;
        \]
  \item $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at 
        every $t$ (so that an open position in $X_n$ has bounded worst-case 
        value in all plausible worlds, before and after settlement).
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \simeq_n v_n.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an affine combination $X = c + \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell \psi_\ell$ we write
$P_t(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell P_t(\psi_\ell)$ for its price under the
market $P$ at time $t$, and $W(X) := c + \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell W(\psi_\ell)$ for
its value in a world $W$.

Suppose toward contradiction that $P_n(X_n) - v_n \not\to 0$. Then there is some
$\varepsilon > 0$ with $|P_n(X_n) - v_n| > \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$,
so at least one of
\[
P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
P_n(X_n) < v_n - \varepsilon
\]
holds for infinitely many $n$. We treat the overpricing case; the underpricing
case is symmetric, with ``sell'' replaced by ``buy'' (the trader then profits
from buying below the settled value rather than selling above it). Assume
$P_n(X_n) > v_n + \varepsilon$ for infinitely many $n$, the \emph{trigger times}.

\paragraph{A continuous selling ramp.}
Define the trade coefficient as a continuous function of the day-$n$ price
$P_n(X_n)$:
\[
\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every

\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has

\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]

and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n v_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]\label{thm:tracking}
\[
A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable; the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
since $m_n^*$ rounds $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, which is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
by the standing assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$. For hypothesis~2: by the
construction of $D_A$, for every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have $\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\
$W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since $C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is
an average of $n$ values $W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have
$W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at every $t$, independently of
consistency.

Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} yields $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n \tfrac{m_n^*}{n}$. By the construction
of $D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n}
\to 0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:vanishing}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable from the information available in $D^n$, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping and admissibility argument are 
unchanged. Since $W(X_n) \in [-B,B]$, a single open sold position opened when 
$P_i(X_i)>\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ has value
\[
\rho_i(P_i(X_i)-W(X_i)) \geq -B,
\]
and a single open bought position opened when $P_i(X_i)<-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$
has value
\[
\rho_i(W(X_i)-P_i(X_i)) \geq -B.
\]
Thus the downside from the at-most-one unsettled position is bounded below by
$-B$. The only substantive change is at settlement: a settled trigger position
opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes $\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$ in the sold
case, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have
$|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger position
($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a bought
one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and the fact
that the settled values vanish. Infinitely many settled triggers then give
plausible net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B$ along a subsequence,
unbounded above, while the downside stays $\geq -B$. This exploits $P$,
contradicting the logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:calibration}
Let $w_n \in [0,1]$ be any $H^+$-generable weight observable at time $n+1$
(e.g.\ any continuous function of the recorded quote $a_n$). Then
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, w_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := w_n a_n - w_n C_n$. Since $w_n$ and $a_n$ are constants observable at
$n+1$ and $Y_n$ is the value of the contract $C_n$ pinned by the settlement
profile, $Z_n$ is a bounded affine combination of the threshold sentences
$\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n|\leq 1$, pinned by $D_H^+$ at $\tau(n):=F(n)+1$
($\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is). Its realized value is
$w_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)$; by Tracking $a_n - Y_n \to 0$ and the profile encodes $Y_n$
up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, so $|w_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)| \leq |a_n-Y_n|+\tfrac{1}{2n}\to 0$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:vanishing} to the shift $\widehat Z_m := Z_{m-1}$ with
$\widehat\tau(m):=F(m-1)+1$ (so $a_{m-1}$ is recorded by time $m$) gives
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[w_n(a_n-Y_n)] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n)\simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
Let $\delta_n$ be an e.c.\ sequence of positive rationals and $p_n$ an
$H^+$-generable sequence of rational probabilities. Writing
$w_n := \mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(a_n > p_n)$ for the soft indicator that $A$ quotes
$P^{(n)}$ above $p_n$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, \mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\, w_n \,\bigr]
\;\succsim_n\;
p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\,w_n\,].
\]
That is: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ with probability at least $p_n$,
$H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ is at least $p_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The weight $w_n$ is $H^+$-generable, lies in $[0,1]$, and is a constant from time
$n+1$ on; it is therefore an admissible conditioning weight for Theorem 4.12.3
(No Expected Net Update under Conditionals) of Garrabrant et al.

\emph{Self-trust.} Applying Theorem 4.12.3 to $H^+$ with the indicator
$\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})$, weight $w_n$, and deferral $m\mapsto F(m-1)$ (a deferral
function since $F(n)>n+1$), and using
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{F(n)}(\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)}))=Y_n$ (Theorem 4.8.6),
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,w_n]
\simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,w_n].
\]
(Because $w_n$ is already settled at $n+1$, this conditional self-trust step in
fact collapses to ordinary self-trust, Theorem 4.12.2 --- the one point at which
our setting is simpler than 4.12.4, whose conditioning event lies in the future.)

\emph{Quote tracks future credence.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:calibration},
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n w_n] \simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n w_n] = a_n w_n$,
swapping $H^+$'s future credence $Y_n$ for $A$'s quote $a_n$; this is the step
that rests on Tracking.

\emph{No false positives.} By Definition 4.3.2, $w_n>0$ forces $a_n>p_n$, so
$a_n w_n \geq p_n w_n$ pointwise (with equality when $w_n=0$). Hence
$a_n w_n \geq p_n w_n = p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[w_n]$, and chaining the three
displays gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Along any subsequence on which $A$ quotes in $[r,s]$ with non-vanishing 
frequency,
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n.
\]
In particular, whenever $A$ quotes within $[r,s]$, $H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ 
comes to lie in $[r,s]$ up to a vanishing error.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
On such a subsequence $G_n$ is bounded below by some $\gamma > 0$, so dividing 
the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:forcedtrust} through by $G_n$ gives 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n$. When $a_n \in [r,s]$ we have $G_n = 1$, so 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$ lies in $[r,s]$ up to an additive error vanishing in $n$.
\end{proof}

\bigskip

The following is a general property of logical inductors, independent of the 
coupled construction.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:projection}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over a language $\mathcal{L} = 
\mathcal{L}_0 \cup \{p\}$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against a 
complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a 
computable deductive process $D$ in which the atom $p$ does not occur. For an 
$\mathcal{L}$-sentence $\chi$, write $\chi^\top$ and $\chi^\bot$ for the $p$-free 
sentences obtained by substituting a fixed tautology, respectively its negation, 
for every occurrence of $p$ in $\chi$. For $c \in (0,1) \cap \mathbb{Q}$ define 
the market $P^c$ over $\mathcal{L}$ by
\[
P^c_n(\chi) := c\,P_n(\chi^\top) + (1-c)\,P_n(\chi^\bot).
\]
Then $P^c$ satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}$ 
relative to $D$, agrees with $P$ on every $p$-free sentence, and 
$P^c_\infty(p) = c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A trade on day $i$ is an affine combination of sentences; write $T_i[\phi]$ for 
its coefficient on $\phi$ (shares bought, negative for sold), so that the trade 
costs $\sum_\phi T_i[\phi]\,P^c_i(\phi)$ at the prevailing prices and pays 
$\sum_\phi T_i[\phi]\,W(\phi)$ in a world $W$.

Because $p$ does not occur in $D$, at every time $t$ the plausible worlds factor 
over the truth value of $p$: writing $\mathrm{PC}_0(D^t)$ for the assignments to 
$p$-free sentences propositionally consistent with $D^t$, every 
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ has the form $(W_0, b)$ with $W_0 \in \mathrm{PC}_0(D^t)$ 
and $b = W(p) \in \{0,1\}$, and \emph{both} extensions $(W_0, 0)$ and 
$(W_0, 1)$ lie in $\mathrm{PC}(D^t)$. By the Shannon expansion 
$\chi \equiv (p \wedge \chi^\top) \vee (\neg p \wedge \chi^\bot)$,
\[
W(\chi) = b\,W_0(\chi^\top) + (1-b)\,W_0(\chi^\bot).
\]

Suppose toward contradiction that a trader $T \in \mathcal{C}$ exploits $P^c$. 
Its holdings after day $n$, valued in a world $(W_0, b)$, are
\[
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, b) = \sum_{i \le n} \sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(W(\phi) - P^c_i(\phi)\bigr).
\]
Define traders $T^\top$ and $T^\bot$ \emph{against $P$} that on each day $i$ 
trade the $p$-free sentences $\phi^\top$, respectively $\phi^\bot$, with the same 
coefficients $T_i[\phi]$ at $P$'s prevailing prices. Since each $P^c_i$ is an 
affine --- hence continuous --- function of the prices of $P$, the coefficients 
$T_i[\phi]$, which are continuous expressible features of the history of $P^c$, 
are continuous expressible features of the history of $P$ of the same rank; the 
substitutions $\phi \mapsto \phi^\top, \phi^\bot$ are computable; and each day 
trades $\operatorname{poly}(i)$ sentences. By closure under polynomial overhead, 
$T^\top, T^\bot \in \mathcal{C}$. Write
\[
V^\top_n(W_0) := W_0\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n} T^\top_i\Bigr) = \sum_{i\le n}\sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(W_0(\phi^\top) - P_i(\phi^\top)\bigr),
\]
and $V^\bot_n(W_0)$ analogously.

Substituting $P^c_i(\phi) = c\,P_i(\phi^\top) + (1-c)P_i(\phi^\bot)$ and 
$W(\phi) = b\,W_0(\phi^\top) + (1-b)W_0(\phi^\bot)$, and adding and subtracting 
$P_i(\phi^\top)$ in the case $b=1$ and $P_i(\phi^\bot)$ in the case $b=0$,
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 1) &= V^\top_n(W_0) + (1-c)\,\Delta_n,\\
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 0) &= V^\bot_n(W_0) - c\,\Delta_n,
\end{align*}
where $\Delta_n := \sum_{i\le n}\sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(P_i(\phi^\top) - P_i(\phi^\bot)\bigr)$ is independent of the 
world. The $c$-weighted combination therefore cancels $\Delta_n$:
\[
c\,\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 1) + (1-c)\,\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 0) 
= c\,V^\top_n(W_0) + (1-c)V^\bot_n(W_0) = W_0\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i\Bigr),
\]
where $\widehat T := c\,T^\top + (1-c)\,T^\bot$ is a single trader against $P$, 
and $\widehat T \in \mathcal{C}$.

Now invoke the assumed exploitation. \emph{Bounded below:} there is $B$ with 
$\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, b) \ge -B$ for all $n$ and all $(W_0, b) \in 
\mathrm{PC}(D^n)$. Since both $(W_0, 0)$ and $(W_0, 1)$ are plausible for every 
plausible $W_0$, the displayed identity gives 
$W_0(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i) \ge -B$ for all $n$ and $W_0$, so the $P$-trader 
$\widehat T$ is bounded below. As $P$ is a logical inductor, $\widehat T$ does 
not exploit it, hence it is also bounded above: 
$W_0(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i) \le B'$ for some $B'$ and all $n, W_0$. 
\emph{Unbounded above:} along some $n_k \to \infty$ there are plausible 
$(W_0^{(k)}, b_k)$ with $\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, b_k) \to +\infty$; pass to 
a subsequence on which $b_k$ is constant, say $b_k = 1$ (the case $b_k = 0$ is 
symmetric, exchanging the roles of $c$ and $1-c$). Then 
$\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) \to +\infty$, and
\[
(1-c)\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 0) 
= W_0^{(k)}\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n_k}\widehat T_i\Bigr) 
- c\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) 
\le B' - c\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) \to -\infty.
\]
As $c < 1$, $\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 0) \to -\infty$, contradicting the 
lower bound $-B$ at the plausible worlds $(W_0^{(k)}, 0)$. Hence no 
$T \in \mathcal{C}$ exploits $P^c$, so $P^c$ satisfies the logical induction 
criterion relative to $D$.

Finally, for $p$-free $\chi$ we have $\chi^\top = \chi^\bot = \chi$, so 
$P^c_n(\chi) = P_n(\chi)$; and $P^c_n(p) = c\,P_n(\top) + (1-c)P_n(\bot) \to c$ 
since $P_n(\top) \to 1$ and $P_n(\bot) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:noncategoricity}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection}, for every $c \in (0,1) \cap 
\mathbb{Q}$ there is a logical inductor over $D$ against $\mathcal{C}$ whose 
limiting credence in $p$ equals $c$ and which agrees with $P$ on every $p$-free 
sentence. In particular, two logical inductors over the same $D$ and the same 
$\mathcal{C}$ can agree on every $p$-free sentence yet assign limiting credences 
$c \neq c'$ to $p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} to obtain $P^c$ and $P^{c'}$; each agrees with 
$P$ off $p$, and $P^c_\infty(p) = c$, $P^{c'}_\infty(p) = c'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If the proposition of interest $P^{(n)}$ is decided by $\Gamma$, then
\[
H_\infty(P^{(n)}) = H^+_\infty(P^{(n)}) = \mathbf{1}[\Gamma \vdash P^{(n)}].
\]
\item Provided $\mathcal{L}$ has a propositional atom occurring in neither 
$\Gamma$ nor $D_H$, the augmented and base limits need not agree: there exist 
such an atom $\phi$, taken as the proposition of interest, and an admissible 
coupled system $(A, H^+)$ --- computable $D_A, D_H^+$ with $A$ a logical inductor 
over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$ and $H^+$ a logical inductor over $D_H^+$ 
against $\mathcal{C}_H$, built from the same $\Gamma$, $D_H$, $\mathcal{C}_H$, 
$\mathcal{C}_A$, $F$, $\sigma$ and satisfying the Tracking and Forced Trust 
theorems --- with
\[
H^+_\infty(\phi) \neq H_\infty(\phi).
\]
Indeed, with $c_0 := H_\infty(\phi) \in (0,1)$ fixed (Theorem 4.6.2, 
Non-Dogmatism, of Garrabrant et al.), every $c \in (0,1) \cap \mathbb{Q}$ is 
realized as $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ by some such system.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) The process $D_H$ is $\Gamma$-complete, and $D_H^+ \supseteq D_H$ is 
$\Gamma$-complete as well; by Theorem 4.2.1 (Provability Induction) of Garrabrant 
et al.\ a logical inductor over a $\Gamma$-complete process assigns limiting 
credence $1$ to $\Gamma$-provable sentences and $0$ to $\Gamma$-refutable ones. 
Hence $H_\infty(\phi)$ and $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ both equal $\mathbf{1}[\Gamma 
\vdash \phi]$.

(ii) Fix such an atom $\phi$ and take it as the proposition of interest, 
$P^{(n)} = \phi$ for all $n$. Run the simultaneous recursion of 
Lemma~\ref{lem:existence}, producing markets $B_A$ over $D_A$ and $B_H$ over 
$D_H^+$ from the fixed \S5 construction, but project each market step: in the 
notation of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection}, with the atom there taken to be $\phi$, 
set $A_t := (B_A)^c_t$ and $H^+_t := (B_H)^c_t$, and use these projected prices 
wherever the construction refers to the markets --- in particular, $D_A$ settles 
contract $n$ using $H^+_{F(n)}(\phi) = (B_H)^c_{F(n)}(\phi)$.

The projection is a computable post-processing of a single market step, so the 
recursion remains well-founded under the same two delays: $D_A^t$ uses 
$H^+_{F(n)}$ only for $\sigma(n) \le t$, hence at times $F(n) < t$, and 
$D_H^{+,t}$ uses the quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$. Because each contract 
$C_n$ is built from threshold symbols, $A_i(C_i) = (B_A)^c_i(C_i) = (B_A)_i(C_i)$, 
so the recorded quotes, and hence $D_H^+$ itself, are exactly those of the base 
construction. All three deductive processes are free of $\phi$, so 
Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} applies to each market: $A = (B_A)^c$ is a logical 
inductor over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$ and $H^+ = (B_H)^c$ is a logical 
inductor over $D_H^+$ against $\mathcal{C}_H$, with $A_\infty(\phi) = 
H^+_\infty(\phi) = c$. Being genuine logical inductors over the constructed 
processes, they satisfy the hypotheses of the Tracking and Forced Trust theorems, 
which apply unchanged. For $c \neq c_0$ this gives $H^+_\infty(\phi) = c \neq c_0 
= H_\infty(\phi)$.
\end{proof}
```

Actually, I'm realizing this is the same problem as in section 4.12.4 — the conditioning weight depends on a future quantity that H⁺ doesn't know yet. And 4.12.4 is proven via 4.12.3, where the weight $w_{f(n)}$ is "the weight as evaluated at the future time $f(n)$." The weight is $\mathbb{P}$-generable — generable sequences can depend on future prices (they're expressible features that get evaluated as the market runs). The expectation $\mathbb{E}_n[\ldots w_{f(n)}]$ is H⁺'s time-$n$ expectation of a LUV that *includes* the future-evaluated weight. But I need to verify that $\mathbf 1(P^{(n)}) w_n$ itself is expressible as a LUV.

Their product is a LUV, and H⁺'s time-$n$ expectation of it is exactly the left-hand side of equation 4.12.4. ✓

For the proof, I'm following 4.12.4's structure through 4.12.3, being careful about how the weight is evaluated at the future time. I apply 4.12.3 with $X_n = \mathbf 1(P^{(n)})$ and $f = F$, where the weight $w_{F(n)} = \mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(\widehat C_n > p_n)$ is evaluated at time $F(n)$. Now I'm checking whether the weight in Theorem 2 refers to the value at time $F(n)$ or at time $n$ itself — the notation $\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(\widehat C_n > p_n)$ describes the feature, but its actual value depends on when $\widehat C_n$ is evaluated, and once we're past time $n+1$, that value is fixed. is fixed. At time $n$, $\widehat C_n$ is the unsettled contract (H⁺'s forecast). 

In the expression $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathbf 1(P^{(n)}) \cdot \mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(\widehat C_n > p_n)]$, the $\widehat C_n$ represents a log-uncertain variable—the contract value treated as random—and the expectation integrates over its eventual realized settlement value. So 4.12.3 establishes that the expectation of the indicator times the settled weight approximates the expectation of $Y_n$ times that weight. The key bridge then connects $Y_n$ to $\widehat C_n$ through two steps: the reflection axiom bounds their difference to $1/(2n)$, which makes the expectation of their difference vanish since the weight is bounded by 1, and then I need to show the expectation of $C_n$ minus $Y_n$ times the weight also goes to zero.

Now I need to bound the expectation $\mathbb{E}_n[(C_n - \widehat C_n)w]$, but this product isn't affine so the vanishing lemma doesn't directly apply—I need to reconsider how to handle the expectation of this product.

Actually, I can reframe this as a weighted vanishing problem: treating $Z = C_n - \widehat C_n$ as an affine LUV with realized value going to zero, and $w$ as a generable weight, the expectation $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[Zw]$ fits the calibration lemma structure. The original calibration lemma handles a similar weighted expectation by applying the vanishing lemma to a constructed affine combination, so I should be able to adapt that approach here.

To apply the vanishing lemma properly, I need the quantity to be computable from the data at the evaluation time. Since $w$ doesn't settle until $n+1$ but I'm evaluating at time $n$, I'll shift the index: define $\widehat X_m := w_{m-1}(C_{m-1} - \widehat C_{m-1})$ evaluated at time $m$, where $w_{m-1}$ is already settled by time $m$. This makes the quantity computable from the available data, so the vanishing lemma gives $H^+_m(\widehat X_m) \simeq_m 0$, which then yields the desired expectation bound.

The issue is that the Tracking relationship between $Y_n$ and $\widehat C_n$ is asymptotic, so the inequality $Y_n \ge p_n$ where $w > 0$ only holds up to vanishing error and isn't something I can prove directly as a hard propositional fact. To make "no false positives" into a provable statement about the settled $\beta$'s, I need to work directly with $\widehat C_n$ instead—that's the quantity actually being thresholded, so the logic becomes airtight. Actually, looking back at 4.12.4, it has exactly this structure—the weight depends on a future price settled later, yet the expectation is evaluated at the earlier time. The proof handles this through 4.12.3, which is specifically designed to relate time-$n$ expectations to future-evaluated quantities with future-settled weights. So future-evaluated weights aren't a problem there; that's the whole mechanism. The real tension is only in my bridge step.

For step (b), I need $\mathbb{E}_n[(C_n - \widehat C_n) w] \to 0$, where the difference is an affine combination and $w$ is a generable weight.
