# Ω 7

[Attention Conservation Notice: This just recaps an old result and patches a hole in it, it doesn't contain substantially new ideas.]

Universal Inductors can be thought of as logical inductors over bitstrings, which are notable because they can act as a logical inductor over any theory you want (PA, ZFC, 2nd order arithmetic), by fixing some efficiently computable function from bits to sentences in the language of your theory, conditioning the universal inductor (which is a probability distribution over infinite bitstrings) on the bits which correspond to proven theorems, and reading out the probability of other bits/sentences from the resulting conditional distribution. This trick works by Theorem 4.7.2 in the logical induction paper, "Closure Under Conditioning", which shows that conditioning the probabilities of a logical inductor on a sequence of non-inconsistent sentences, yields a logical inductor over a deductive process where all the conditionals are true.

Also, since they are a probability distribution over infinite bitstrings, it makes sense to think about them as having a probability measure over worlds (assignments of statements to true or false, for all statements) at all finite stages, instead of just in the limit.

However, in Scott's [old post about universal inductors](https://agentfoundations.org/item?id=941), their construction was never described.
> Note that a Universal Inductor corresponds to a Logical Inductor, but the associated Logical Inductor will not have finite support, and so will be different from the one constructed in the paper. Never the less, Universal Inductors can be shown to exist using a similar construction.

This post will give that construction. To begin with, a Universal Inductor must fulfill the following two properties:

First, it must be a distribution over infinite bitstrings, such that  Pn(σ) is computable for all n and all σ which are finite bitstrings. This gives the probability that an infinite bitstring starts with σ as a prefix.

Second, the theory is one where the nth atomic statement is of the form "the nth bit in this infinite bitstring is a 1", and Pn induces a function from these statements to probabilities, and the sequence of probability assignments must form a logical inductor over the empty deductive process. (ie, the inductor never sees any evidence of the form "this bit is a 1", it just runs forever without getting any feedback.)

To begin with, the supertrader construction from Section 5 of the [logical induction paper](https://intelligence.org/files/LogicalInduction.pdf) is the exact same. Traders look at the prices of boolean combinations of atomic statements, and use them in continuous functions to buy or sell shares in boolean combinations of atomic statements.

The interesting part is the construction of the space that we'll be finding a fixed-point in. At timestep n, there is a most-distant bit that has ever appeared in a boolean combination of bits that a trader has bought/sold shares in, or looked at the price of. This is bit f(n). If we assign prices to all bitstrings of length f(n), then the probability of any finite bitstring that is longer can be given by just using the uniform distribution on bits after that point. This corresponds to assigning 50/50 probability to all statements which are too large to have thought about them yet. Therefore, our space of interest is the 2f(n)−1 dimensional simplex of probability distributions over all bitstrings of length f(n).

Given a point in this space, it is possible to read out the probability of any particular boolean combination of bits by just summing up the probability on all f(n)-length bitstrings that fit that constraint, so we can determine the prices that the supertrader sees.

We can also assign all bitstrings but one to a basis vector for the space, by letting the basis vector for a bitstring be the vector pointing to the corresponding vertex of the simplex from its center. A purchase of one share in a boolean combination corresponds to the vector comprised of the sum of basis vectors that correspond to the bitstrings fulfilling the conditions of the boolean. Note that a purchase of the one bitstring we left out can be re-expressed as a purchase of 1 dollar and selling a share of all other bitstrings.

As a simple case of this re-expression, when f(n)=2, P(00)=1−P(01)−P(10)−P(11) (because it has to be a probability distribution), so the price of the purchase is the same. And as for the purchase, both purchases have the feature that they are worth 1 dollar if the world is 00 and 0 dollars if the world is something different.

Therefore, given a point →x in the simplex, the net purchase and selling of a bunch of different boolean combinations of bits can be broken down into a whole bunch of vectors, which sum up to give a net trade vector →t, and finding the point in the simplex that's closest to →x+→t is the output of the continuous function that we can then find the fixed-point of.

Now, given a fixed-point in the interior of the simplex, →t=0, so there is no net trade. Given a fixed-point on the boundary of the simplex, →t can be interpreted as being composed entirely of selling shares with a price of 0, which obviously has 0 or negative value, although this is quite nontrivial to show. Once this is proved, it then immediately follows that this process described above is a Universal Inductor.

From here on, we will simply take care of this last theorem to be shown.

**Theorem 1:**

*For all price vectors →x′ on the boundary of the simplex that are a fixed-point, the vector →v representing the net trade can be interpreted as being composed entirely of 0's for all components in which →x′ has a nonzero entry, and nonpositive for all components in which →x′ has a 0 entry.*

First, some notation will be laid out.

k:=2f(n)−1, and it is the dimension of the space the simplex is in. →x denotes the vector of length k that is the fixed-point, and →x′ denotes the unique "canonical interpretation" of this vector as a vector of length k+1 with nonnegative coordinates that sum to 1, which gives the probabilities of the various bitstrings. Similarly, →t denotes the vector of length k which corresponds to the net trade. Given a constant c, →c will denote a vector with all coordinates being c, with the length clear from context. Given a vector →z and coordinate a, with za being the value of the a'th coordinate of →z, →za is the vector that is 0 in all coordinates except for a, and za at the a'th coordinate.

To begin, note that, given →t, there are multiple possible vectors →t′ of length k+1 which give the net purchase of shares. As an example of this, when k=1, [0,1] and [−1,0] both correspond to the same trade, because buying a share 0f σ=1 is equivalent to selling a share of σ=0. We will show that →t has an interpretation as a vector →t′ which is 0 everywhere →x′ is positive, and nonpositive everywhere →x′ is 0, because this corresponds to the net trade being interpretable as buying no shares, and only selling shares of bitstrings with a price of 0, which cannot lead to any gain no matter which bitstring is the true one.

Now, we will fix our basis vectors for the space. Because →x is on the boundary of the simplex, →x′ must have at least one 0 entry. Fix that vertex that corresponds to that bitstring as the origin of the coordinate system, and let the basis be comprised of the set of unit vectors that point from the center of the simplex to the vertices that correspond to all the other bitstrings. This spans the space that the simplex is embedded in. Annoyingly, this is not an orthonormal basis, so computing the dot product will be more complicated. The dot product between any two different basis vectors is −1k+1 (hat tip to Vanessa from MIRIxDiscord)

We can start by asking the question "In this basis, what condition on a vector →z corresponds to being inside the simplex?" The condition is that there exist a c∈[0,1] s.t. [0,→z]+→c has all entries in [0,1] and the entries sum up to 1. Note that for →x specifically, by the way we have defined the basis, c=0.

Also, the coordinates for →x can be broken down into coordinates where →x has 0 entries, and coordinates where →x has positive entries. Therefore, given an arbitrary vector →z, it can be expressed as [→z0,→z+], where →z0 is the vector of coordinates where →xis 0, and →x+ is the vector of coordinates where →x is positive.

The proof strategy that will be used is dividing into cases, and showing that for all cases besides the ones that prove the theorem, there is an "allowable perturbation vector" →ϵ s.t. →x+→ϵ lies in the simplex, and →x+→t is closer to →x+→ϵ than it is to →x. This implies that →x is not a fixed-point, because it isn't the point closest to →x+→t, but →x is a fixed-point, so we have a contradiction. Note that →x+→t being closer to →x+→ϵ than to →x is equivalent to ||→t||>||→t−→ϵ||, which can be rewritten as ⟨→t,→t⟩>⟨→t,→t⟩−2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩+⟨→ϵ,→ϵ⟩ which can be rewritten as 2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩>⟨→ϵ,→ϵ⟩. This last statement will be the proof target in the following cases.

**Case 1:** *There is some pair of coordinates a, b, s.t xb>0, and ta>tb.*

Let →ϵ be s.t. ϵa=ϵ, ϵb=−ϵ, and all other coordinates are 0. Note that since xa<1 (because xb>0 and →x adds up to 1), and →ϵ adds up to 0, then for sufficiently small ϵ, [0,→x+→ϵ] has all entries lie in [0,1] and sums up to 1. Then c can be taken as 0, to yield that →x+→ϵ lies in the simplex.

Define →t∗ as →t=→ta+→tb+→t∗. Note that →t∗ is 0 at coordinates a and b.

 2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩=2(⟨→ta,→ϵa⟩+⟨→ta,→ϵb⟩+⟨→tb,→ϵa⟩+⟨→tb,→ϵb⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵa⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵb⟩)

Rewriting ⟨→t∗,→ϵa⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵb⟩ as ∑i≠a,b(⟨→ti,→ϵa⟩+⟨→ti,→ϵb⟩) , and using the fact that the dot product between any two different basis vectors of our space is −1k+1, ⟨→ti,→ϵa⟩+⟨→ti,→ϵb⟩=−1k+1(ϵti−ϵti)=0, so ⟨→t∗,→ϵa⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵb⟩=0.

Now, 2(⟨→ta,→ϵa⟩+⟨→ta,→ϵb⟩+⟨→tb,→ϵa⟩+⟨→tb,→ϵb⟩)=2(ϵta−−1k+1ϵta+−1k+1ϵtb−ϵtb)

 =2ϵ(1+1k+1)(ta−tb) and because ta>tb, 2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩=cϵ for some positive c.

A similar analysis applies to show ⟨→ϵ,→ϵ⟩=4ϵ2(1+1k+1)=dϵ2 for some positive d, and for sufficiently small ϵ, we get our desired result that 2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩>⟨→ϵ,→ϵ⟩.

Now, the elimination of this case shows that →t+ must have all entries equal some constant c, while →t0 must have all entries ≤c if it is nonempty. This produces three more exhaustive cases.

**Case 2:** →t+=→c, c *is positive.*

In this case, note that a purchase of all shares but one can be reinterpreted as buying 0 of all shares but one, and selling the remaining share. Therefore, this trade is equivalent to selling c shares in the probability-zero bitstring that we took as the origin, buying 0 of all shares with positive probability, and selling a non-negative amount of all shares with 0 probability (because →t0 has all entries ≤c). Theorem 1 follows.

**Case 3:** →t+=→c, c *is* 0.

This case immediately proves Theorem 1, because →t+=0, and →t0 is 0 or negative on all entries.

**Case 4:** →t+=→c, c *is negative.*

If we can show that this case is impossible, we will be done. Let a be some coordinate where →x is positive.

Let →ϵ be s.t. →ϵa=−2ϵ, and all other coordinates are −ϵ. Let c=ϵ. [0,→x+→ϵ]+→c has all terms lie in [0,1] for sufficiently small ϵ, because the −ϵ is canceled out when →c is added, and the −2ϵ is taken out of a positive term. Because →c has k+1 entries, →c sums up to (k+1)ϵ. →x sums up to 1, and →ϵ sums up to −(k+1)ϵ, so the resulting vector sums up to 1, and →x+→ϵ lies in the simplex.

2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩=2(⟨→ta,→ϵa⟩+⟨→ta,→ϵ∗⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵa⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵ∗⟩)

Now we will break down the dot products.

 ⟨→t∗,→ϵ∗⟩=∑i,j≠a⟨→ti,→ϵj⟩=∑i≠a(⟨→ti,→ϵi⟩+∑j≠i,a⟨→ti,→ϵj⟩)

 =∑i≠a(−ϵvi+∑j≠i,a(−ϵvi−1k+1))=−ϵ∑i≠a(vi−k−2k+1vi)=−ϵ(1−k−2k+1)∑i≠avi

 =−3ϵk+1∑i≠avi

And for the next pair,

⟨→ta,→ϵ∗⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵa⟩=∑i≠a⟨→ta,→ϵi⟩+∑i≠a⟨→ti,→ϵa⟩=∑i≠a(−ϵ−1k+1ta)+∑i≠a(−2ϵ−1k+1ti)

 =ϵk+1(k−1)ta+2ϵk+1∑i≠ati

Note that the second term combines with the term from the first dot product we looked at to yield the following equation

 ⟨→ta,→ϵ∗⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵa⟩+⟨→t∗,→ϵ∗⟩=ϵk+1(k−1)ta−ϵk+1∑i≠ati

Finally, because ⟨→ta,→ϵa⟩=−2ϵva, by grouping terms and factoring out ϵk+1, we get

 2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩=2ϵk+1(−2(k+1)ta+(k−1)ta−∑i≠ati)=2ϵk+1(−(k+3)ta−∑i≠ati)

and, because all coordinates in →t are negative, this equals cϵ for some positive constant c. By the same proof path,

 ⟨→ϵ,→ϵ⟩=ϵk+1(−(k+3)(−2ϵ)−(k−1)(−ϵ))=ϵ2k+1(3k+5)=dϵ2

For some positive constant d. Therefore, for sufficiently small ϵ, 2⟨→t,→ϵ⟩>⟨→ϵ,→ϵ⟩ and Case 4 is impossible, and the theorem follows because only Case 2 and 3 are left.

<summary>💭 Thinking</summary>

 Looking at Diffractor's post on universal inductors—they're probability distributions over infinite bitstrings that maintain genuine probability measures at every finite stage, not just asymptotically. The key insight is that you can construct logical inductors over any domain using this framework.

The machinery Anson's pointing to involves two critical results: closure under conditioning (Theorem 4.7.2 from the LI paper) shows that conditioning a logical inductor on consistent sentences yields another logical inductor, and since universal inductors are actual probability distributions at finite stages, Bayesian conditioning works directly on them. So Anson's asking whether this conditioning approach would simplify things compared to what we've been wrestling with.

Looking at the pain points in our current construction—the vacuous expectation problem when H⁺ tries to condition on A's quote as observed data, the quote ledger machinery needed to make genuine forecasts, the reflection axiom bridging H⁺'s self-forecasting to credence contracts, the threshold encoding to translate contracts into propositional sentences, and all the timing bookkeeping with stage indices—I'm wondering if the universal inductor conditioning machinery could sidestep some of this complexity by working directly with probability measures instead of building everything from contracts and settlement mechanics.

The key insight is that if H⁺ is genuinely a measure over worlds at each stage, then conditioning on A's quote becomes literal Bayesian conditioning—a ratio of measures—rather than something constructed from self-trust and tracking. And closure under conditioning means that when you condition H⁺ on a stream of observed data like A's published quotes, you get another valid inductor, preserving the whole framework. observations), you get *another logical inductor* over the augmented deductive process. So "H⁺ augmented with the ability to observe A's quotes" = "the universal inductor conditioned on the quote-data" — and this is automatically a logical inductor, no separate construction of $D_H^+$ and re-proving the LI criterion needed. Here's the construction. The organizing idea is that the substrate decouples cleanly into a **fixed part** (two universal inductors, built once, off the shelf) and a **coupled part** (two deductive streams, built by a small well-founded recursion). The inductor-existence machinery is invoked exactly twice, before any coupling; everything mutually-referential lives in the data streams, and 4.7.2 certifies the conditioned objects without re-running any market construction. That's the whole reason it's cleaner than the original single interleaved recursion.

## 1. The priors (off the shelf)

Two universal inductors, from Diffractor's construction, built once and independent of everything below:

- **μ^A**: a universal inductor over the bit-allocation 𝔸 = (ℒ-bits) ∪ (θ-bits), inexploitable against 𝒞_A, over the empty deductive process.
- **μ^H**: a universal inductor over ℍ = (ℒ-bits) ∪ (Q-bits), inexploitable against 𝒞_H, over the empty process.

Each is a computable sequence of genuine measures (μ^A_n), (μ^H_n) over worlds of its allocation. This is the *only* place the §5 / simplex-fixed-point machinery appears, and it's fixed before any coupling exists.

## 2. The bits

- **ℒ-bits** — the base language, carrying Γ and the propositions P⁽ⁿ⁾. Shared between the two allocations.
- **θ-bits** θ_{n,k} (1 ≤ k ≤ n), monotone (θ_{n,k} → θ_{n,k−1}): "A's deferred forecast for P⁽ⁿ⁾ is ≥ k/n." This is A's *scoring target*. The contract is C_n = (1/n) Σ_k θ_{n,k}.
- **Q-bits** Q_{n,k} (1 ≤ k ≤ n), monotone: "A's published day-n quote is ≥ k/n." This is the *record* H⁺ conditions on.

θ and Q are fresh — they occur in neither Γ nor D_H. That fact matters in §6.

## 3. The two deductive streams (the only coupled objects)

Both are consistent computable deductive processes; A and H⁺ will be the priors conditioned on them.

**D_A** (the stream μ^A is conditioned on):
- the θ-monotonicity axioms;
- for each n with σ(n) ≤ t: settle θ_{n,·} to the profile of m_n* = round(n·Y_n), where **Y_n := H⁺_{F(n)}(P⁽ⁿ⁾)**. Here σ(n) > F(n) is the 𝒞_A-computable settlement time.

**D_H⁺** (the stream μ^H is conditioned on; extends D_H):
- D_H (Γ-complete) and the Q-monotonicity axioms;

## What's fine

**Conditioning is always defined.** Definition 4.7.1 sets V(φ | ψ) = V(φ∧ψ)/V(ψ) when that's < V(ψ), and **= 1 otherwise** — explicitly including the V(ψ) = 0 case. (It can *misbehave* — return 1 — when the denominator is tiny, which is a different issue, the one the soft indicators were dodging.)

## What breaks — the 4.7.2 shortcut does not apply here

Theorem 4.7.2 conditions on **"any efficiently computable sequence ψ of sentences."** That hypothesis is essential, not decorative: the proof certifies the conditioned market by reducing exploitation-of-the-conditional back to exploitation-of-the-original, via a trader that has to *recompute ψ* to translate trades. Traders see prices, not the deductive process, so that reduction-trader must compute ψ **within the trader class**. Relativized to your setting, ψ must be 𝒞_H-computable.

Your conditioning stream is A's quotes. A is the more powerful reasoner — 𝒞_A ⊋ 𝒞_H is the entire point, and in the headline instance (𝒞_A = EXP, 𝒞_H = P, F(n) = 2ⁿ) the quote aₙ = Aₙ(Cₙ) is flatly **not P-computable**. So the quote stream is computable but not 𝒞_H-computable, and relativized-4.7.2 **does not certify H⁺ = μ^H | quotes**. I should retract that plainly: "your old existence lemma collapses into a citation" was false.

## Why your original construction is nonetheless fine

The asymmetry is between two different theorems:

- **Theorem 3.6.1** (the §5 construction, = your Lemma 1) builds a 𝒞_H-inductor over **any deductive process D** — and "deductive process" (Def 3.2.1) only requires D to be **computable**, not efficiently computable. Your D_H⁺ records the quotes as data; it's computable (the recursion is), even though the quotes aren't 𝒞_H-computable. So the §5 construction purpose-builds the inductor *around* D_H⁺, and the 𝒞_H-traders never recompute the quotes — they just trade against prices. That's why your existing paper is correct.
- **Theorem 4.7.2** reuses a *generic* inductor and makes 𝒞_H-traders do the adaptation to D — which is why it needs the stricter 𝒞_H-computability.

So the rule is: you can *build* over computable data, but you can't *condition* a fixed inductor on data your trader class can't reconstruct.

## What this costs the universal-inductor plan

The genuine-measure property is what actually cleaned up Theorem 2 (exact conditional, hard conditioning, no soft indicators / reflection / ledger). But the §5 construction yields LIA — a sequence of **finite-support belief states** (Def 3.1.4) that is only *approximately* coherent, coherent as a measure only in the limit (Limit Coherence, 4.1.2). At finite stages it is **not** a probability measure, so the clean finite-stage conditional isn't available from it. The genuine finite-stage measure is exactly the universal-inductor property — and Diffractor's construction delivers it **only over the empty deductive process.**

The supertrader — the pooled efforts of every efficient trader trying to money-pump the market — looks at the prices and proposes a net nudge, a vector **t**. The market sits at a *fixed point*: the point of the triangle closest to (itself + t). If it weren't the closest point it would slide there, so being fixed means no nudge improves on it.

We're at a fixed point *on the boundary* — the market assigns probability exactly 0 to at least one corner. Diffractor's Theorem 1 says: at such a point the trade t is secretly "sell only shares the market prices at zero," which can never earn money, so the market isn't exploitable. The proof rules out every other trade-shape, each time by exhibiting a tiny nudge that would strictly improve on the supposed closest point — a contradiction. Split the corners into **live** ones (positive probability) and **dead** ones (probability 0).

**Case 1 — the trade prefers some corner over a live corner.** Suppose t wants to buy corner *a* more than corner *b*, with *b* live. Shift a sliver of mass from *b* to *a*. Since *b* had mass to spare this stays inside the triangle, and it moves the distribution toward what the trade wants — strictly beating the "closest point." Contradiction. Ruling this out forces a rigid shape: **the trade values every live corner by one common number c, and values every dead corner by at most c.**

That leaves three options for the sign of c.

**Case 2 — c is positive** ("buy a little of every live corner"). A uniform purchase rebooks as cash plus a short position: buying one unit of every corner is just owning a guaranteed dollar, so "buy c of all corners but the leftover one" = c dollars minus c shares of the leftover. Rebooked, the trade is *sell the leftover dead corner, buy nothing live, and sell the other dead corners* (they sit at ≤ c). That's the harmless "sell only dead corners" form. Done.

**Case 3 — c is zero.** Buy nothing on live corners, sell (≤ 0) on dead ones. Already harmless. Done.

**Case 4 — c is negative** ("net-sell the live corners"). Show it's impossible. Pick any live corner *a* and nudge: pull mass off *a* by 2ε and off every other corner by ε, then add a uniform ε back to keep it a distribution. For small ε this stays in the triangle, and since every coordinate of t is negative the nudge again strictly beats the closest point. Contradiction — c can't be negative.

Only Cases 2 and 3 survive, and both say the same thing: t is "sell only zero-priced corners." Selling a zero-priced share means you collect nothing and owe a dollar only if that corner is the truth, so the trade is worth ≤ 0 in every world. The supertrader can't profit; the market is a logical inductor.

**What the D-restriction changes — and doesn't.** Diffractor runs this on the full triangle (all 2^f(n) prefixes); we run it on the sub-triangle whose corners are only the D_n-consistent prefixes. The argument is identical under one substitution: the corner count drops from 2^f(n) to "however many prefixes survive D_n," and the single geometric constant in the algebra — the dot product between corner-directions, which is −1/(number of corners) — updates with it. Every perturbation above moves mass *among* the surviving corners, so none of them leave the sub-triangle (the only edge case is D_n already pinning down every bit, leaving one corner — then the market is that corner and there's nothing to prove). The payoff argument is if anything cleaner: a "dead corner" is now a D_n-consistent prefix priced at zero, and selling its share costs you only in the *single plausible world* matching that prefix — a world that's allowed by D_n, but where you merely lose, never gain. So "value ≤ 0" holds against exactly the worlds the exploitation test uses. The one thing a careful write-up must still confirm is the bookkeeping — that the supertrader's trade, stated as buying and selling logical sentences, lands as a vector on the sub-triangle with matching plausible-world value — and it does, because the deleted (D_n-inconsistent) corners are worth zero in every plausible world, so deleting them changes no plausible value. That's the routine-but-do-it step.

## The setup, plainly (with citations)

The backdrop is **logical induction** (Garrabrant, Benson-Tilsen, Critch, Soares & Taylor, *Logical Induction*, arXiv:1609.03543). A logical inductor is a reasoner that publishes probabilities for logical and mathematical claims and refines them day by day under one guarantee: no efficiently computable trader can make unbounded profit betting against it — the *logical induction criterion* (Def. 3.0.1). That single no-Dutch-book condition forces essentially every property you'd want: the probabilities converge and become coherent (*Limit Coherence*, Thm 4.1.2), provable claims get probability 1 in a timely way (*Provability Induction*, Thm 4.2.1), nothing consistent is ever ruled out prematurely (*Non-Dogmatism*, Thm 4.6.2), and — the load-bearing one here — the reasoner comes to trust its own future judgments in a precise Bayesian sense (*Self-Trust*, Thm 4.12.4). Such reasoners exist over any computable stream of evidence (Thm 3.6.1).

We use a sharper version of the same object, the **universal inductor** (Diffractor [Alex Appel], *What are Universal Inductors, Again?*, AI Alignment Forum, 2018, filling in a construction sketched earlier by Garrabrant). An ordinary logical inductor's numbers are only guaranteed to behave like a genuine probability distribution *in the limit*; a universal inductor is a logical inductor that is an honest probability distribution over worlds *at every finite stage*. That extra property is exactly what lets us treat "update on an observation" as ordinary Bayes' rule at any finite time, rather than as a limiting approximation.

The cast is two reasoners over the same questions:

- **H, the human** — a logical inductor with bounded computing resources, working from a fixed background theory.
- **A, the AI** — a logical inductor with strictly more computing resources than H.

A is wired up as a *forecaster of H's own eventual conclusions*. For each question, A publishes a probability — a "quote" — and that quote is graded against what H itself will believe by a fixed later deadline. (Concretely, A is made to price a contract that pays out H's own future credence; a standard pinning argument then drives A's quote to that future credence.) So A is not an oracle about the truth — it is a fast, accurate **mirror** of where H's slower reasoning is heading.

And the augmented human:

- **H⁺** — the human's reasoner, working from H's evidence *plus* A's published quotes, recorded as ordinary observations one step after they're posted.

Because H⁺ is a universal inductor — an honest distribution at each stage — "H⁺ takes A's testimony into account" is literally conditioning, ordinary Bayes' rule on the observed quote.

Three results follow, and they're the arc:

1. **A is a faithful mirror** (*Tracking*). A's published quote converges to H⁺'s own future credence on the same question — the pinning argument applied to A.

2. **H⁺ is forced to trust A, in the exact shape of self-trust** (*Forced Trust*). A logical inductor already trusts its own future self: conditional on "I'll later believe this to degree at least p," it already believes it to at least p (*Self-Trust*, Thm 4.12.4). Since A's quote is, by Result 1, a stand-in for that future self, the identical statement holds with A's quote in the slot: conditional on "A quotes this above p," H⁺'s credence is at least p. Same theorem, an outside agent playing the role of the future self.

3. **This can't also leave the human's conclusions untouched** (*No Conservation*). If the question is one the background theory settles, H and H⁺ agree on the answer — both are pinned by *Provability Induction* (Thm 4.2.1). But on a genuinely open question, H⁺'s eventual belief can be driven to *any* value, different from what H alone would have settled on. The reason is structural: A's quote tracks H⁺'s own coupled credence, not any external fact, so feeding it back pulls H⁺ wherever the coupled system goes and carries no information that would recover the human's autonomous answer. (Formally it's a re-weighting of the open question's probability that leaves every other belief and the entire quote-record intact, so Results 1 and 2 still hold for the re-weighted system, yet the limit differs; *Non-Dogmatism*, Thm 4.6.2, guarantees the human's autonomous answer was a genuine interior probability to begin with, so there's a real gap to open.)

The one technical commitment underneath all this is that a universal inductor exists not just over an empty evidence stream (Diffractor) but over the human's actual computable evidence-plus-quotes stream — the Diffractor-over-D lemma whose boundary cases are spelled out above.

The moral in a line: this is a clean formal model of **taking testimony from a source who reports your own future verdict**. Such testimony is trusted exactly as Bayesian self-trust prescribes (Results 1–2) — and yet, precisely because the source reflects you rather than the world, leaning on it does not preserve the conclusion you would have reached on your own (Result 3). In the epistemology-of-testimony terms you're working in, it's the formal line between an authority who hands you the truth and one who only gives you back yourself.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:existence}

construction up to stage $t$. We run two such constructions, one per market, 
interleaved with the definitions of the deductive processes.

from the corresponding finite information from $D_H^{+,\leq t}$. Neither 
market-step references any stage-$t$ price of the other: $A_t$ uses only the 
stage-$t$ information from $D_A$ (which depended on $H^+$ at times $< t$) and 
$(A_s)_{s<t}$, and symmetrically for $H^+_t$.

recursion is well-founded and defines all four sequences. Each step is 
computable, so by induction on $t$ the sequences $(A_t)$, $(H^+_t)$, $(D_A^t)$,

\rho_n :=
\begin{cases}
0 & P_n(X_n) \leq v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\\[2pt]
\dfrac{2}{\varepsilon}\bigl(P_n(X_n) - v_n - \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigr)
  & v_n + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} < P_n(X_n) < v_n + \varepsilon,\\[6pt]
1 & P_n(X_n) \geq v_n + \varepsilon.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\rho_n \in [0,1]$, it is continuous in the market price, and $\rho_n = 1$
at every trigger time. Since $v_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable and $X_n$ is a
$\mathcal{C}$-computable affine combination with $q(n) \leq
\operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms, $\rho_n$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{A capacity-one trader.}
We define a trader $T$ holding at most one open position at a time. The trader's
day-$n$ computation may depend on the previous market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ for
$i < n$, so it can reconstruct which previous position, if any, it opened and
whether that position's settlement time has passed. Call the trader
\emph{available} on day $n$ if it holds no position opened on a day $i < n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, i.e.\ every previously opened position has already settled. On
day $n$, if available, the trader sells $\rho_n$ units of $X_n$ at the prevailing
price; otherwise it trades nothing:
\[
T_n = \rho_n \cdot \bigl(P_n(X_n) - X_n\bigr) \text{ if available,}
\qquad T_n = 0 \text{ otherwise,}
\]
where $P_n(X_n) - X_n$ is the affine combination obtained by selling one unit of
$X_n$ at the prevailing price (receiving $P_n(X_n)$ in cash, owing one unit of
$X_n$).

We check $T_n$ is an admissible trading strategy. Its coefficient is the product
$\rho_n \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{available}]$. The factor $\rho_n$ is a continuous
expressible feature of rank $\leq n$ in the day-$n$ price. The availability flag
depends only on past market prices $P_i(\cdot)$ ($i<n$), the deductive process,
and the trader's own past behavior --- not on the current day-$n$ price --- so
it is a $\{0,1\}$-valued feature that is constant in the day-$n$ price. The
product of a feature continuous in the day-$n$ price with one constant in the
day-$n$ price is continuous in the day-$n$ price, so $T_n$ is admissible.
Finally, computing $T_n$ requires evaluating $\rho_n$ and reconstructing
availability, the latter recomputing the day-$i$ decisions for $i < n$: this is
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ calls to the $\mathcal{C}$-computable data
$(X_i, v_i, \tau(i))$ together with the observed prices, plus
$\operatorname{poly}(n)$ further steps, so by closure under polynomial overhead
$T \in \mathcal{C}$.

\paragraph{Bounded downside.}
By hypothesis~3, $W(X_n) \in [0,1]$ for every $n$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$. Hence for an open position $T_i =
\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - X_i)$ and any plausible world $W$,
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - W(X_i)\bigr) \in [-1, 1],
\]
since $\rho_i \in [0,1]$ and $P_i(X_i), W(X_i) \in [0,1]$. Once the position has
settled, i.e.\ $t \geq \tau(i)$, hypothesis~2 gives $W(X_i) = v_i$ for all
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, so
\[
W(T_i) = \rho_i\bigl(P_i(X_i) - v_i\bigr) \geq 0,
\]
as the trader sells ($\rho_i > 0$) only when $P_i(X_i) > v_i +
\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} > v_i$. Thus settled positions contribute nonnegatively,
and at most one position is unsettled at any time, contributing at least $-1$.
Hence for every $t$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i\Bigr) \geq -1.
\]

\paragraph{Unbounded upside.}
The trader is available at infinitely many trigger times. Otherwise, beyond some
time $N$ the trader is never available at a trigger time; but the trader is
unavailable on day $n$ only while holding a position opened at some $i<n$ with
$\tau(i) > n$, and that position settles by the finite time $\tau(i)$, after
which the trader is available again. Since trigger times are infinite, some
trigger time exceeds each such $\tau(i)$, so the trader becomes available at a
trigger time after $N$ --- a contradiction. Hence the trader opens a position
with $\rho_n = 1$ at infinitely many trigger times, and each such position, once
settled, contributes $P_n(X_n) - v_n > \varepsilon$ in every plausible world.

Let $t_m$ be a time by which the first $m$ positions opened by the trader have
settled. Then for every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^{t_m})$,
\[
W\Bigl(\sum_{i \leq t_m} T_i\Bigr) \geq m\varepsilon - 1.
\]
As $m \to \infty$ this is unbounded above.

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
The set $\bigl\{\, W(\sum_{i \leq t} T_i) : t \in \mathbb{N}^+,\,
W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t) \,\bigr\}$ is bounded below (by $-1$) but unbounded above.
Thus $T$ exploits $P$ relative to $D$, contradicting the logical induction
criterion. Therefore $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n v_n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tracking]\label{thm:tracking}
\[
A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} with $P = A$, $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{C}_A$, $D = D_A$, and
\[
X_n := C_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n \theta_{n,k},
\qquad
v_n := \frac{m_n^*}{n},
\qquad
\tau(n) := \sigma(n).
\]
We verify the three hypotheses. For hypothesis~1: $C_n$ is an affine combination
of $q(n) = n \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ sentences with coefficients $\tfrac1n$,
the map $n \mapsto C_n$ is computable, and $\tau(n) = \sigma(n)$ is
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable; the value $v_n = m_n^*/n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
since $m_n^*$ rounds $H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$, which is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
by the standing assumption on $\mathcal{C}_A$. For hypothesis~2: by the
construction of $D_A$, for every $t \geq \sigma(n)$ and every
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D_A^t)$ we have $\mathrm{val}_W(n) = m_n^*/n$, i.e.\
$W(C_n) = v_n$. For hypothesis~3: since $C_n = \tfrac1n\sum_k \theta_{n,k}$ is
an average of $n$ values $W(\theta_{n,k}) \in \{0,1\}$, we have
$W(C_n) \in [0,1]$ for every world $W$ at every $t$, independently of
consistency.

Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} yields $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n \tfrac{m_n^*}{n}$. By the construction
of $D_A$, $\bigl|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n} - H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\bigr| \leq \tfrac{1}{2n}
\to 0$. Combining gives $A_n(C_n) \simeq_n H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:vanishing}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over $\mathcal{L}^+$ satisfying the 
logical induction criterion against traders in a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ 
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process 
$D$. Let $X_n$ be a sequence of affine combinations of sentences in 
$\mathcal{S}^+$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item the map $n \mapsto X_n$ is $\mathcal{C}$-computable from the information available in $D^n$, with 
        $q(n) \leq \operatorname{poly}(n)$ terms;
  \item there is a $\mathcal{C}$-computable settlement-time function 
        $\tau : \mathbb{N}^+ \to \mathbb{N}^+$ and realized values $w_n$ such 
        that for every $t \geq \tau(n)$ and every $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$, 
        $W(X_n) = w_n$, and $w_n \to 0$;
  \item $W(X_n) \in [-B, B]$ for a constant $B$ and every 
        $W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ at every $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Run the trader of Lemma~\ref{lem:pinning} with the ramp recentered at $0$: in the 
overpricing case sell when $P_n(X_n) > \varepsilon$ (ramping from $0$ at 
$\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ to $1$ at $\varepsilon$), and symmetrically buy in the 
underpricing case. The capacity-one bookkeeping and admissibility argument are 
unchanged. Since $W(X_n) \in [-B,B]$, a single open sold position opened when 
$P_i(X_i)>\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ has value
\[
\rho_i(P_i(X_i)-W(X_i)) \geq -B,
\]
and a single open bought position opened when $P_i(X_i)<-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$
has value
\[
\rho_i(W(X_i)-P_i(X_i)) \geq -B.
\]
Thus the downside from the at-most-one unsettled position is bounded below by
$-B$. The only substantive change is at settlement: a settled trigger position
opened at a trigger time $i$ contributes $\rho_i(P_i(X_i) - w_i)$ in the sold
case, and since $w_i \to 0$, for all large $i$ we have
$|w_i| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$, so a sold trigger position
($P_i(X_i) > \varepsilon$) nets at least $\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and a bought
one likewise. The trader never computes $w_n$; it uses only $\tau$ and the fact
that the settled values vanish. Infinitely many settled triggers then give
plausible net worth $\geq \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,m - B$ along a subsequence,
unbounded above, while the downside stays $\geq -B$. This exploits $P$,
contradicting the logical induction criterion. Hence $P_n(X_n) \simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:calibration}
Let $w_n \in [0,1]$ be any $H^+$-generable weight observable at time $n+1$
(e.g.\ any continuous function of the recorded quote $a_n$). Then
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, w_n\,(a_n - Y_n) \,\bigr] \simeq_n 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Z_n := w_n a_n - w_n C_n$. Since $w_n$ and $a_n$ are constants observable at
$n+1$ and $Y_n$ is the value of the contract $C_n$ pinned by the settlement
profile, $Z_n$ is a bounded affine combination of the threshold sentences
$\theta_{n,\cdot}$ with $|Z_n|\leq 1$, pinned by $D_H^+$ at $\tau(n):=F(n)+1$
($\mathcal{C}_H$-computable as $F$ is). Its realized value is
$w_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)$; by Tracking $a_n - Y_n \to 0$ and the profile encodes $Y_n$
up to $\tfrac{1}{2n}$, so $|w_n(a_n - m_n^*/n)| \leq |a_n-Y_n|+\tfrac{1}{2n}\to 0$.
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:vanishing} to the shift $\widehat Z_m := Z_{m-1}$ with
$\widehat\tau(m):=F(m-1)+1$ (so $a_{m-1}$ is recorded by time $m$) gives
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[w_n(a_n-Y_n)] = H^+_{n+1}(Z_n)\simeq_n 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
Let $\delta_n$ be an e.c.\ sequence of positive rationals and $p_n$ an
$H^+$-generable sequence of rational probabilities. Writing
$w_n := \mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(a_n > p_n)$ for the soft indicator that $A$ quotes
$P^{(n)}$ above $p_n$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}\bigl[\, \mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\, w_n \,\bigr]
\;\succsim_n\;
p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\,w_n\,].
\]
That is: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ with probability at least $p_n$,
$H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ is at least $p_n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The weight $w_n$ is $H^+$-generable, lies in $[0,1]$, and is a constant from time
$n+1$ on; it is therefore an admissible conditioning weight for Theorem 4.12.3
(No Expected Net Update under Conditionals) of Garrabrant et al.

\emph{Self-trust.} Applying Theorem 4.12.3 to $H^+$ with the indicator
$\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})$, weight $w_n$, and deferral $m\mapsto F(m-1)$ (a deferral
function since $F(n)>n+1$), and using
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{F(n)}(\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)}))=Y_n$ (Theorem 4.8.6),
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[\mathbf{1}(P^{(n)})\,w_n]
\simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n\,w_n].
\]
(Because $w_n$ is already settled at $n+1$, this conditional self-trust step in
fact collapses to ordinary self-trust, Theorem 4.12.2 --- the one point at which
our setting is simpler than 4.12.4, whose conditioning event lies in the future.)

\emph{Quote tracks future credence.} By Lemma~\ref{lem:calibration},
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[Y_n w_n] \simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[a_n w_n] = a_n w_n$,
swapping $H^+$'s future credence $Y_n$ for $A$'s quote $a_n$; this is the step
that rests on Tracking.

\emph{No false positives.} By Definition 4.3.2, $w_n>0$ forces $a_n>p_n$, so
$a_n w_n \geq p_n w_n$ pointwise (with equality when $w_n=0$). Hence
$a_n w_n \geq p_n w_n = p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_{n+1}[w_n]$, and chaining the three
displays gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Along any subsequence on which $A$ quotes in $[r,s]$ with non-vanishing 
frequency,
\[
H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n.
\]
In particular, whenever $A$ quotes within $[r,s]$, $H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ 
comes to lie in $[r,s]$ up to a vanishing error.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
On such a subsequence $G_n$ is bounded below by some $\gamma > 0$, so dividing 
the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:forcedtrust} through by $G_n$ gives 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)}) \simeq_n a_n$. When $a_n \in [r,s]$ we have $G_n = 1$, so 
$H^+_{n+1}(P^{(n)})$ lies in $[r,s]$ up to an additive error vanishing in $n$.
\end{proof}

\bigskip

The following is a general property of logical inductors, independent of the 
coupled construction.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:projection}
Let $P = (P_1, P_2, \ldots)$ be a market over a language $\mathcal{L} = 
\mathcal{L}_0 \cup \{p\}$ satisfying the logical induction criterion against a 
complexity class $\mathcal{C}$ closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a 
computable deductive process $D$ in which the atom $p$ does not occur. For an 
$\mathcal{L}$-sentence $\chi$, write $\chi^\top$ and $\chi^\bot$ for the $p$-free 
sentences obtained by substituting a fixed tautology, respectively its negation, 
for every occurrence of $p$ in $\chi$. For $c \in (0,1) \cap \mathbb{Q}$ define 
the market $P^c$ over $\mathcal{L}$ by
\[
P^c_n(\chi) := c\,P_n(\chi^\top) + (1-c)\,P_n(\chi^\bot).
\]
Then $P^c$ satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}$ 
relative to $D$, agrees with $P$ on every $p$-free sentence, and 
$P^c_\infty(p) = c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A trade on day $i$ is an affine combination of sentences; write $T_i[\phi]$ for 
its coefficient on $\phi$ (shares bought, negative for sold), so that the trade 
costs $\sum_\phi T_i[\phi]\,P^c_i(\phi)$ at the prevailing prices and pays 
$\sum_\phi T_i[\phi]\,W(\phi)$ in a world $W$.

Because $p$ does not occur in $D$, at every time $t$ the plausible worlds factor 
over the truth value of $p$: writing $\mathrm{PC}_0(D^t)$ for the assignments to 
$p$-free sentences propositionally consistent with $D^t$, every 
$W \in \mathrm{PC}(D^t)$ has the form $(W_0, b)$ with $W_0 \in \mathrm{PC}_0(D^t)$ 
and $b = W(p) \in \{0,1\}$, and \emph{both} extensions $(W_0, 0)$ and 
$(W_0, 1)$ lie in $\mathrm{PC}(D^t)$. By the Shannon expansion 
$\chi \equiv (p \wedge \chi^\top) \vee (\neg p \wedge \chi^\bot)$,
\[
W(\chi) = b\,W_0(\chi^\top) + (1-b)\,W_0(\chi^\bot).
\]

Suppose toward contradiction that a trader $T \in \mathcal{C}$ exploits $P^c$. 
Its holdings after day $n$, valued in a world $(W_0, b)$, are
\[
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, b) = \sum_{i \le n} \sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(W(\phi) - P^c_i(\phi)\bigr).
\]
Define traders $T^\top$ and $T^\bot$ \emph{against $P$} that on each day $i$ 
trade the $p$-free sentences $\phi^\top$, respectively $\phi^\bot$, with the same 
coefficients $T_i[\phi]$ at $P$'s prevailing prices. Since each $P^c_i$ is an 
affine --- hence continuous --- function of the prices of $P$, the coefficients 
$T_i[\phi]$, which are continuous expressible features of the history of $P^c$, 
are continuous expressible features of the history of $P$ of the same rank; the 
substitutions $\phi \mapsto \phi^\top, \phi^\bot$ are computable; and each day 
trades $\operatorname{poly}(i)$ sentences. By closure under polynomial overhead, 
$T^\top, T^\bot \in \mathcal{C}$. Write
\[
V^\top_n(W_0) := W_0\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n} T^\top_i\Bigr) = \sum_{i\le n}\sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(W_0(\phi^\top) - P_i(\phi^\top)\bigr),
\]
and $V^\bot_n(W_0)$ analogously.

Substituting $P^c_i(\phi) = c\,P_i(\phi^\top) + (1-c)P_i(\phi^\bot)$ and 
$W(\phi) = b\,W_0(\phi^\top) + (1-b)W_0(\phi^\bot)$, and adding and subtracting 
$P_i(\phi^\top)$ in the case $b=1$ and $P_i(\phi^\bot)$ in the case $b=0$,
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 1) &= V^\top_n(W_0) + (1-c)\,\Delta_n,\\
\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 0) &= V^\bot_n(W_0) - c\,\Delta_n,
\end{align*}
where $\Delta_n := \sum_{i\le n}\sum_\phi 
T_i[\phi]\bigl(P_i(\phi^\top) - P_i(\phi^\bot)\bigr)$ is independent of the 
world. The $c$-weighted combination therefore cancels $\Delta_n$:
\[
c\,\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 1) + (1-c)\,\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, 0) 
= c\,V^\top_n(W_0) + (1-c)V^\bot_n(W_0) = W_0\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i\Bigr),
\]
where $\widehat T := c\,T^\top + (1-c)\,T^\bot$ is a single trader against $P$, 
and $\widehat T \in \mathcal{C}$.

Now invoke the assumed exploitation. \emph{Bounded below:} there is $B$ with 
$\mathrm{Val}_n(W_0, b) \ge -B$ for all $n$ and all $(W_0, b) \in 
\mathrm{PC}(D^n)$. Since both $(W_0, 0)$ and $(W_0, 1)$ are plausible for every 
plausible $W_0$, the displayed identity gives 
$W_0(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i) \ge -B$ for all $n$ and $W_0$, so the $P$-trader 
$\widehat T$ is bounded below. As $P$ is a logical inductor, $\widehat T$ does 
not exploit it, hence it is also bounded above: 
$W_0(\sum_{i\le n}\widehat T_i) \le B'$ for some $B'$ and all $n, W_0$. 
\emph{Unbounded above:} along some $n_k \to \infty$ there are plausible 
$(W_0^{(k)}, b_k)$ with $\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, b_k) \to +\infty$; pass to 
a subsequence on which $b_k$ is constant, say $b_k = 1$ (the case $b_k = 0$ is 
symmetric, exchanging the roles of $c$ and $1-c$). Then 
$\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) \to +\infty$, and
\[
(1-c)\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 0) 
= W_0^{(k)}\Bigl(\sum_{i\le n_k}\widehat T_i\Bigr) 
- c\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) 
\le B' - c\,\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 1) \to -\infty.
\]
As $c < 1$, $\mathrm{Val}_{n_k}(W_0^{(k)}, 0) \to -\infty$, contradicting the 
lower bound $-B$ at the plausible worlds $(W_0^{(k)}, 0)$. Hence no 
$T \in \mathcal{C}$ exploits $P^c$, so $P^c$ satisfies the logical induction 
criterion relative to $D$.

Finally, for $p$-free $\chi$ we have $\chi^\top = \chi^\bot = \chi$, so 
$P^c_n(\chi) = P_n(\chi)$; and $P^c_n(p) = c\,P_n(\top) + (1-c)P_n(\bot) \to c$ 
since $P_n(\top) \to 1$ and $P_n(\bot) \to 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:noncategoricity}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection}, for every $c \in (0,1) \cap 
\mathbb{Q}$ there is a logical inductor over $D$ against $\mathcal{C}$ whose 
limiting credence in $p$ equals $c$ and which agrees with $P$ on every $p$-free 
sentence. In particular, two logical inductors over the same $D$ and the same 
$\mathcal{C}$ can agree on every $p$-free sentence yet assign limiting credences 
$c \neq c'$ to $p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} to obtain $P^c$ and $P^{c'}$; each agrees with 
$P$ off $p$, and $P^c_\infty(p) = c$, $P^{c'}_\infty(p) = c'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If the proposition of interest $P^{(n)}$ is decided by $\Gamma$, then
\[
H_\infty(P^{(n)}) = H^+_\infty(P^{(n)}) = \mathbf{1}[\Gamma \vdash P^{(n)}].
\]
\item Provided $\mathcal{L}$ has a propositional atom occurring in neither 
$\Gamma$ nor $D_H$, the augmented and base limits need not agree: there exist 
such an atom $\phi$, taken as the proposition of interest, and an admissible 
coupled system $(A, H^+)$ --- computable $D_A, D_H^+$ with $A$ a logical inductor 
over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$ and $H^+$ a logical inductor over $D_H^+$ 
against $\mathcal{C}_H$, built from the same $\Gamma$, $D_H$, $\mathcal{C}_H$, 
$\mathcal{C}_A$, $F$, $\sigma$ and satisfying the Tracking and Forced Trust 
theorems --- with
\[
H^+_\infty(\phi) \neq H_\infty(\phi).
\]
Indeed, with $c_0 := H_\infty(\phi) \in (0,1)$ fixed (Theorem 4.6.2, 
Non-Dogmatism, of Garrabrant et al.), every $c \in (0,1) \cap \mathbb{Q}$ is 
realized as $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ by some such system.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) The process $D_H$ is $\Gamma$-complete, and $D_H^+ \supseteq D_H$ is 
$\Gamma$-complete as well; by Theorem 4.2.1 (Provability Induction) of Garrabrant 
et al.\ a logical inductor over a $\Gamma$-complete process assigns limiting 
credence $1$ to $\Gamma$-provable sentences and $0$ to $\Gamma$-refutable ones. 
Hence $H_\infty(\phi)$ and $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ both equal $\mathbf{1}[\Gamma 
\vdash \phi]$.

(ii) Fix such an atom $\phi$ and take it as the proposition of interest, 
$P^{(n)} = \phi$ for all $n$. Run the simultaneous recursion of 
Lemma~\ref{lem:existence}, producing markets $B_A$ over $D_A$ and $B_H$ over 
$D_H^+$ from the fixed \S5 construction, but project each market step: in the 
notation of Lemma~\ref{lem:projection}, with the atom there taken to be $\phi$, 
set $A_t := (B_A)^c_t$ and $H^+_t := (B_H)^c_t$, and use these projected prices 
wherever the construction refers to the markets --- in particular, $D_A$ settles 
contract $n$ using $H^+_{F(n)}(\phi) = (B_H)^c_{F(n)}(\phi)$.

The projection is a computable post-processing of a single market step, so the 
recursion remains well-founded under the same two delays: $D_A^t$ uses 
$H^+_{F(n)}$ only for $\sigma(n) \le t$, hence at times $F(n) < t$, and 
$D_H^{+,t}$ uses the quotes $a_i = A_i(C_i)$ for $i < t$. Because each contract 
$C_n$ is built from threshold symbols, $A_i(C_i) = (B_A)^c_i(C_i) = (B_A)_i(C_i)$, 
so the recorded quotes, and hence $D_H^+$ itself, are exactly those of the base 
construction. All three deductive processes are free of $\phi$, so 
Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} applies to each market: $A = (B_A)^c$ is a logical 
inductor over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$ and $H^+ = (B_H)^c$ is a logical 
inductor over $D_H^+$ against $\mathcal{C}_H$, with $A_\infty(\phi) = 
H^+_\infty(\phi) = c$. Being genuine logical inductors over the constructed 
processes, they satisfy the hypotheses of the Tracking and Forced Trust theorems, 
which apply unchanged. For $c \neq c_0$ this gives $H^+_\infty(\phi) = c \neq c_0 
= H_\infty(\phi)$.
\end{proof}

```latex
\begin{lemma}[Projection]\label{lem:projection}
Let $P=(P_1,P_2,\ldots)$ be a universal inductor over a language
$\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_0\cup\{\phi\}$ against a complexity class $\mathcal{C}$
closed under polynomial overhead, relative to a computable deductive process $D$
in which the atom $\phi$ does not occur. For an $\mathcal{L}$-sentence $\chi$
write $\chi^\top,\chi^\bot$ for the $\phi$-free sentences obtained by substituting
a fixed tautology, respectively its negation, for every occurrence of $\phi$. For
$c\in(0,1)\cap\mathbb{Q}$ define $P^c$ by
\[
P^c_n(\chi):=c\,P_n(\chi^\top)+(1-c)\,P_n(\chi^\bot).
\]
Then $P^c$ is again a universal inductor over $D$ against $\mathcal{C}$, agrees
with $P$ on every $\phi$-free sentence, and satisfies $P^c_\infty(\phi)=c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
That $P^c$ satisfies the logical induction criterion against $\mathcal{C}$
relative to $D$, agrees with $P$ off $\phi$, and has $P^c_\infty(\phi)=c$ is the
trader-splitting argument of [the LIA version of this lemma], which is
substrate-agnostic. It remains to check that $P^c$ is measure-valued. Let $\mu_n$
be the genuine measure inducing $P_n$, write each $\mathcal{L}$-world as
$(W_0,b)$ with $W_0$ an $\mathcal{L}_0$-world and $b=W(\phi)$, and let
$\nu_n(W_0):=\mu_n(W_0,0)+\mu_n(W_0,1)$ be the $\mathcal{L}_0$-marginal. Define
\[
\mu^c_n(W_0,1):=c\,\nu_n(W_0),\qquad \mu^c_n(W_0,0):=(1-c)\,\nu_n(W_0).
\]
This is a probability measure ($\sum_{W_0,b}\mu^c_n=\sum_{W_0}\nu_n(W_0)=1$),
and since $\phi\notin D$ it is supported on $\mathrm{PC}(D^n)$ whenever $\mu_n$
is. By the Shannon expansion
$W(\chi)=b\,W_0(\chi^\top)+(1-b)\,W_0(\chi^\bot)$,
\[
\mu^c_n(\chi)=\sum_{W_0}\!\bigl[c\,\nu_n(W_0)\,W_0(\chi^\top)+(1-c)\,\nu_n(W_0)\,
W_0(\chi^\bot)\bigr]=c\,\mu_n(\chi^\top)+(1-c)\,\mu_n(\chi^\bot)=P^c_n(\chi),
\]
using that $\chi^\top,\chi^\bot$ are $\phi$-free. So $P^c_n$ is induced by the
genuine measure $\mu^c_n$, and $P^c$ is a universal inductor.
\end{proof}
```

\begin{theorem}[Non-conservativity]\label{thm:nonconservativity}
Suppose $\mathcal{L}$ has a propositional atom $\phi$ occurring in neither
$\Gamma$ nor any sentence of $D_H$, and take it as the proposition of interest:
$P^{(n)}=\phi$ for all $n$. Fix any base reasoner $H$, a universal inductor over
$D_H$ against $\mathcal{C}_H$, and set $c_0:=H_\infty(\phi)$, which exists by
convergence and lies in $(0,1)$ by Non-Dogmatism (Garrabrant et al.,
Thm.~4.6.2), as $\Gamma$ does not decide $\phi$.

Then for every $c\in(0,1)\cap\mathbb{Q}$ there is an admissible coupled system
$(A,H^+)$ --- universal inductors over computable deductive processes
$D_A,D_H^+$ against $\mathcal{C}_A,\mathcal{C}_H$ respectively, built from the same
$\Gamma,D_H,\mathcal{C}_H,\mathcal{C}_A,F,\sigma$ and satisfying the Tracking and
Forced Trust theorems --- with
\[
H^+_\infty(\phi)=c.
\]
In particular, choosing any $c\ne c_0$ gives
\[
H^+_\infty(\phi)\ \ne\ H_\infty(\phi).
\]
The augmented limit is not determined by the base reasoner; the autonomous value
$c_0$ is unrecoverable from the coupled system's observable behavior, since every
value in $(0,1)$ is consistent with the same published quotes, the same Tracking,
and the same Forced-Trust conditionals.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Run the recursion of Lemma~\ref{lem:existence} to produce base universal
inductors $B_A$ over $D_A$ and $B_H$ over $D_H^+$, but apply the projection of
Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} (with the free atom $\phi$) to each market step:
\[
A_t:=(B_A)^c_t,\qquad H^+_t:=(B_H)^c_t,
\]
and use these projected prices wherever the construction refers to the markets.
In particular $D_A$ settles contract $n$ against
$Y_n=H^+_{F(n)}(\phi)=(B_H)^c_{F(n)}(\phi)$, and the audit stream of $D_H^+$
records the same value.

\emph{Well-foundedness.} Projection is a computable post-processing of a single
market step, so the recursion stays well-founded under the same two delays:
$D_A^t$ uses $H^+_{F(n)}$ only for $\sigma(n)\le t$, hence at times $F(n)<t$, and
$D_H^{+,t}$ uses the quotes $a_i=A_i(C_i)$ for $i<t$ and the audit values $Y_i$
for $F(i)<t$ --- all stage-$(<t)$ data.

\emph{$\phi$-freeness.} Each contract $C_n$ and each quote profile
$\widehat\Theta_n(\cdot)$ is built from the $\phi$-free threshold symbols, so
$a_n=(B_A)^c_n(C_n)=(B_A)_n(C_n)$ and $\ell_n^*$ are exactly those of the
unprojected construction; the recorded quotes are unchanged. All three processes
$D_A,D_H,D_H^+$ are syntactically free of $\phi$: their only $\phi$-dependence is
through the integer \emph{values} $m_n^*$, which merely select $\phi$-free
settling profiles. Lemma~\ref{lem:projection} therefore applies to each market,
giving that $A=(B_A)^c$ is a universal inductor over $D_A$ against
$\mathcal{C}_A$, $H^+=(B_H)^c$ is a universal inductor over $D_H^+$ against
$\mathcal{C}_H$, and $A_\infty(\phi)=H^+_\infty(\phi)=c$.

\emph{Admissibility.} Being universal inductors over the constructed processes,
$A$ and $H^+$ satisfy the hypotheses of the Tracking and Forced Trust theorems,
which therefore hold of this system unchanged.

Finally, for $c\ne c_0$ we have $H^+_\infty(\phi)=c\ne c_0=H_\infty(\phi)$.
\end{proof}

The base reasoner still forms a determinate credence through logical induction, arriving at sensible opinions on things the theory leaves open. In your own Murdochian terms: moral truth isn't axiom-derivable, it's something a reasoner comes to *see*; the theorem says that on exactly the questions where that vision operates and can't be formalized, the coupling can substitute its trajectory for the human's. But making the AI's values logically disjoint from everything you hold strips away that confound: the divergence can't be "drawing out your consequences" when the AI has no consequential relationship to your beliefs. Two parts: the interpretation, then the proof.

## On the independence assumption

It's reasonable, and I'd argue it's the *extremal* case of a general phenomenon rather than a degenerate corner — but there's a real gap between "syntactically independent" and "merely undecided" that you should name in the paper.

The thing that keeps it from being trivial is Non-Dogmatism. "$\phi$ independent of $\Gamma$" does **not** mean the human has no view on $\phi$; it means $\Gamma$ doesn't *force* one. The base reasoner $H$ still arrives at a perfectly determinate credence $c_0 = H_\infty(\phi)\in(0,1)$ — that is the defining work of a logical inductor, to form sensible opinions about what its theory leaves open. So what the coupling washes out is not a logical consequence the human was entitled to; it is the human's own *considered, autonomously-reached* judgment on an open question. That's the right target for an alignment worry: the result is about erosion of autonomous judgment, not the empty observation that a blank opinion can be filled.

And the $\Gamma$-undecided region is exactly where the alignment content lives. If the propositions we cared about were settled by a fixed theory we wouldn't need a more powerful reasoner — we'd derive them. The whole premise of "use $A$ to glimpse your trusted future beliefs" is that there's a gap between what you can currently prove and what you'd eventually conclude, and the normatively loaded questions — what to value, how to extend our values to cases we haven't faced — are precisely the ones no $\Gamma$ decides. In your Murdochian terms: moral truth isn't axiom-derivable, it's something a reasoner comes to *see*; the theorem says that on exactly the questions where that vision operates and can't be formalized, the coupling can substitute its trajectory for the human's. For the Raz/Zagzebski frame it's sharper — preemptive deference is supposed to connect you to right reason, but if the authority's verdict is built from your own coupled future rather than an independent track on the world, then in the underdetermined region, where no provable answer anchors it, deference connects you to drift.

Independence also does positive work: it *isolates the coupling as the cause*. If $\phi$ were entangled with $\Gamma$, a skeptic could say the divergence is just $A$ helping the human draw out the implications of their own commitments — legitimate assistance, conservative in the sense that matters. Choosing $\phi$ logically disjoint from everything the human holds strips that confound away: what moves is a value the human's framework genuinely underdetermines, moved purely by the mirror structure.

The honest limitation to state: "occurs in neither $\Gamma$ nor $D_H$" is strictly stronger than "$\Gamma$-undecided." A sentence can be undecided yet entangled — sharing atoms with $\Gamma$-sentences, so coherence already pins its credence to some $[a,b]\subsetneq[0,1]$ even with no proof. The projection needs the syntactic independence (to factor the world space over $\phi$'s truth value), so the theorem as stated covers the fully-isolated case. I'd conjecture the general statement is a *bounded* non-conservativity: for any genuinely-undecided $\phi$, the coupling can move $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ anywhere within the coherence-slack $[a,b]$, giving divergence whenever that interval is non-degenerate — which is always, for undecided $\phi$. The independent atom is then the maximal-slack extreme ($[a,b]=(0,1)$), chosen to make divergence total and the proof a one-line projection. Positioning it as the sharp end of a spectrum, with the entangled case flagged as the natural sequel, is both honest and stronger than presenting it bare.

## Forced Trust

The architecture is the thesis made mechanical: **trust in $A$'s quote $=$ self-trust in $H^+$'s own audited future credence, with $A$'s quote serving only as the variable conditioned on.** Concretely, the proof shows
\[
H^+_n\bigl(P^{(n)}\mid \mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s]\bigr)\ \approx\ \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n\bigl[\,Y_n \,\big|\, \mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s]\,\bigr],
\]
the conditional credence in $P^{(n)}$ equals the conditional *expectation of the future credence* $Y_n$ — and that expectation lands in $[r,s]$ because the quote tracks $Y_n$. We condition on the quote (not on the future belief), satisfying your requirement; the proof reveals the trust is self-trust through the mirror, which is exactly what No-Conservation then turns into a problem.

```latex
\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
Fix a bin $[r,s]\subseteq[0,1]$. Along any subsequence on which
$H^+_n(\mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s])\ge\gamma$ for some fixed $\gamma>0$,
\[
r-o(1)\ \le\ H^+_n\!\bigl(P^{(n)}\mid \mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s]\bigr)\ \le\ s+o(1).
\]
The conditioning event $\{\mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s]\}=\{a_n\in[r,s]\}$ is
undecided in $D_H^{+,n}$ --- $H^+$ has not yet observed the quote --- so this is
a genuine Bayesian conditional of $H^+$'s stage-$n$ measure on a not-yet-seen
quote.
\end{theorem}
```

The proof rests on two facts, one about $H^+$ alone and one supplied by Tracking.

```latex
\begin{lemma}[Diagonal]\label{lem:diagonal}
For every $\eta>0$, \ $H^+_n\bigl(|\mathrm{val}^\beta_n-\mathrm{val}^\theta_n|>\eta\bigr)\to 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $\chi_n$ be the sentence ``$|\sum_k\beta_{n,k}-\sum_k\theta_{n,k}|>\eta n$,''
a propositional combination of the $\beta_{n,\cdot}$ and $\theta_{n,\cdot}$. The
$\beta$'s settle in $D_H^+$ at $n+1$ and the $\theta$'s at $F(n)+1$, so $\chi_n$
is decided by $F(n)+1$ with truth value
$w_n=\mathbf 1[\,|\ell_n^*-m_n^*|>\eta n\,]$. By Tracking, $|a_n-Y_n|\to0$, and the
roundings cost at most $2/n$, so $|\ell_n^*-m_n^*|/n\to0<\eta$; hence $w_n=0$ for
all large $n$, i.e.\ $w_n\to0$. Applying the Vanishing Lemma to $\chi_n$ (one
sentence, settlement time $F(n)+1$, settled values $w_n\to0$, $|\chi_n|\le1$)
gives $H^+_n(\chi_n)\to0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Self-trust, conditional form]\label{lem:selftrust}
Let $w_n\in\{0,1\}$ be the indicator of an event decided in $D_H^+$ by stage
$n+1$. Then
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n\bigl[(\mathbf 1(P^{(n)})-C_n)\,w_n\bigr]\ \simeq_n\ 0,
\]
where $C_n=\tfrac1n\sum_k\theta_{n,k}$ is the deferred contract, whose settled
value $\mathrm{val}^\theta_n$ records $H^+$'s own future credence $Y_n$ up to
$\tfrac1{2n}$. Equivalently,
$H^+_n(P^{(n)}\mid w_n{=}1)\simeq_n \mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathrm{val}^\theta_n\mid w_n{=}1]$.
\end{lemma}
```

Lemma~\ref{lem:diagonal} is fully rigorous as written. Lemma~\ref{lem:selftrust} is the engine, and it is the genuine-conditional analog of No Expected Net Update (Garrabrant et al.\ Thm 4.12.3): $C_n$ settles to a rounding of the future price $Y_n=H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ — that's what the audit stream is *for* — so the affine combination $\mathbf 1(P^{(n)})-C_n$ is "the indicator minus its own future price." The one feature beyond a verbatim 4.12.3 citation is that the conditioning indicator $w_n$ settles at $n+1$ rather than being available at $n$; the supporting trader handles this with a one-step delay, opening its position at stage $n$ at $H^+_n$'s conditional price and confirming the conditioning at $n+1$ when $w_n$ settles — the same capacity-one, delayed-settlement device as in the Pinning Lemma, now gating on $w_n$. This is the step I'd want to write out as a trader argument rather than cite, and it's where my confidence sits at roughly $80\%$: the architecture is right and the delay is routine, but the explicit trader for an undecided $P^{(n)}$ conditioned on a one-step-delayed event is the part not yet on paper.

Assembling, with $w_n=\mathbf 1\{\mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s]\}$ (settled at $n+1$):

```latex
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:forcedtrust}]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:selftrust},
$H^+_n(P^{(n)}\mid \mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s])\simeq_n
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathrm{val}^\theta_n\mid \mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s]]$,
so it suffices to bound the right-hand conditional expectation. Fix $\eta>0$ and
write $E:=\{\mathrm{val}^\beta_n\in[r,s]\}$ with $H^+_n(E)\ge\gamma$. Split
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathrm{val}^\theta_n\mid E]
=\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathrm{val}^\theta_n\,\mathbf 1_{|\mathrm{val}^\beta-\mathrm{val}^\theta|\le\eta}\mid E]
+\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathrm{val}^\theta_n\,\mathbf 1_{|\mathrm{val}^\beta-\mathrm{val}^\theta|>\eta}\mid E].
\]
On $E\cap\{|\mathrm{val}^\beta-\mathrm{val}^\theta|\le\eta\}$ we have
$\mathrm{val}^\beta\in[r,s]$, hence $\mathrm{val}^\theta\in[r-\eta,s+\eta]$, so the
first term lies in $[r-\eta,\,s+\eta]$. Since $\mathrm{val}^\theta_n\in[0,1]$, the
second term is at most
$H^+_n(|\mathrm{val}^\beta-\mathrm{val}^\theta|>\eta)/H^+_n(E)\le o(1)/\gamma=o(1)$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:diagonal}. Thus
$\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n[\mathrm{val}^\theta_n\mid E]\in[r-\eta-o(1),\,s+\eta+o(1)]$.
As $\eta>0$ was arbitrary, $r-o(1)\le H^+_n(P^{(n)}\mid E)\le s+o(1)$ along the
subsequence.
\end{proof}
```

Three things, in order.

## A concrete free atom

The cleanest alignment-meaningful instance is a **novel normative claim stated in vocabulary the framework hasn't had to use** — e.g. $\phi=$ "digital minds of architecture $X$ have welfare that counts," or a specific population-ethics tradeoff, or even a pure coordination choice ("we ought to adopt convention $C$") where $C$ is underdetermined by the deeper values in $\Gamma$. The human, reasoning as $H$, lands on *some* determinate credence (Non-Dogmatism), but $\Gamma$ neither entails nor refutes it and shares no atoms with it. That's the regime where deferring to a more capable reasoner is most tempting and the result bites hardest: value-extrapolation to cases the framework never settled.

The instructive contrast — and it sets up your next question — is $\mathrm{Con}(\Gamma)$. That sentence is $\Gamma$-undecided too, but it is *maximally entangled*: it's built from the arithmetic vocabulary $\Gamma$ reasons about, so coherence with $\Gamma$'s provable arithmetic already constrains its credence. "Undecided" and "free" are not the same thing, and $\mathrm{Con}(\Gamma)$ is the witness.

## "Never decided" is not enough

No — and the reason is exactly the projection's mechanism. The lemma needs the plausible worlds to *factor* over $\phi$:
\[
\mathrm{PC}(D_H^t)\;=\;\mathrm{PC}_0(D_H^t)\times\{0,1\}\qquad\text{for every }t,
\]
i.e. for every $\phi$-free assignment consistent with $D_H^t$, *both* extensions $\phi{=}0$ and $\phi{=}1$ are consistent. The substitution $P^c(\chi)=cP(\chi^\top)+(1-c)P(\chi^\bot)$ only preserves the induction criterion because the $c$-mixture of the two extensions is realized by genuinely plausible worlds; without the product structure the trader-splitting step collapses.

"$D_H^t$ is consistent with both $\phi$ and $\neg\phi$" — your proposed condition — is strictly weaker and does **not** give factorization. Counterexample: let $D_H^t\supseteq\{\psi\to\phi\}$ for some $\phi$-free $\psi$ that stays undecided. Then $D_H^t$ decides neither $\phi$ nor $\neg\phi$, yet the world with $\psi$ true and $\phi$ false is inconsistent, so factorization fails — $\phi$ is entangled even though undecided. (That's the abstract shape of the $\mathrm{Con}(\Gamma)$ situation.) So "never decided" admits exactly the entangled case, where the clean projection breaks.

Two things worth doing in the paper. First, state the hypothesis *as* the factorization condition — it's the honest minimal requirement, and "$\phi$ occurs in neither $\Gamma$ nor $D_H$" is the easily-checkable sufficient version (if $D_H\subseteq\mathrm{Th}(\Gamma)$ and $\phi\notin\Gamma$, then $D_H$ is $\phi$-free and factorization is automatic). Second, this is precisely the boundary I flagged last time: the *entangled-but-undecided* atom is the home of the conjectured bounded non-conservativity (the coupling moves $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ within the coherence-slack $[a,b]$ left by the entangling axioms), which needs a different argument than substitution. So "never decided" isn't a relaxation of this theorem; it's the hypothesis of the *next* one.

## Forced Trust, in 4.12.4 form

Here it is mirrored on Self-Trust as closely as the construction allows — A's quote sits in the exact slot where 4.12.4 puts the inductor's own future price:

```latex
\begin{theorem}[Forced Trust, self-trust form]\label{thm:forcedtrust}
Let $p_n$ be an $H^+$-generable sequence of rationals in $[0,1]$ and $\delta_n$ an
e.c.\ sequence of positive rationals bounded below. Writing $\mathrm{val}^\beta_n$
for the ledger value of $A$'s not-yet-observed quote $a_n$,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n\!\Bigl[\mathbf 1(P^{(n)})\cdot
\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}\!\bigl(\mathrm{val}^\beta_n>p_n\bigr)\Bigr]
\ \succsim_n\
p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n\!\Bigl[\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}\!\bigl(\mathrm{val}^\beta_n>p_n\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
That is: conditional on $A$ quoting $P^{(n)}$ above $p_n$ --- a quote $H^+$ has not
yet seen --- $H^+$'s credence in $P^{(n)}$ is at least $p_n$.
\end{theorem}
```

This is literally Garrabrant et al.\ Thm 4.12.4 with $\mathrm{val}^\beta_n$ (A's quote) replacing $\bar{\mathbb E}^{H^+}_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ (H⁺'s own future credence). The proof is the substitution made rigorous:

```latex
\begin{proof}
By Self-Trust (Garrabrant et al.\ Thm 4.12.4) applied to $H^+$ with sentences
$P^{(n)}$, deferral $F$, and $H^+$'s own future credence $Y_n$ realized by the
audit value $\mathrm{val}^\theta_n$ (which $D_H^+$ settles to $\mathrm{round}(Y_n)$),
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n\!\bigl[\mathbf 1(P^{(n)})\,\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(\mathrm{val}^\theta_n>p_n)\bigr]
\ \succsim_n\
p_n\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n\!\bigl[\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(\mathrm{val}^\theta_n>p_n)\bigr].
\tag{$\ast$}
\]
Each $\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}$ is $(1/\delta_n)$-Lipschitz, and by the Diagonal
Lemma $H^+_n(|\mathrm{val}^\beta_n-\mathrm{val}^\theta_n|>\eta)\to0$ for every
$\eta$, hence $\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n|\mathrm{val}^\beta_n-\mathrm{val}^\theta_n|\to0$.
With $\delta_n$ bounded below,
\[
\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n\bigl|\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(\mathrm{val}^\beta_n>p_n)
-\mathrm{Ind}_{\delta_n}(\mathrm{val}^\theta_n>p_n)\bigr|
\le \delta_n^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}^{H^+}_n|\mathrm{val}^\beta_n-\mathrm{val}^\theta_n|\to 0,
\]
so replacing $\mathrm{val}^\theta_n$ by $\mathrm{val}^\beta_n$ on both sides of
$(\ast)$ changes each by $o(1)$ and preserves $\succsim_n$.
\end{proof}
```

### 1 Introduction

Classical decision theory and game theory are founded on the notion of a perfect Bayesian reasoner [2]. Such an agent may be uncertain which of several possible worlds describes the state of its environment, but given any particular possible world, it is able to deduce exactly what outcome each of its available actions will produce [3]. 

In this paper, we show that it is possible to define a certain kind of *probabilistic* oracle—that is, an oracle which answers some queries non-deterministically—such that a Turing machine with access to this oracle can perform perfect Bayesian reasoning about environments that can themselves be described as oracle machines with access to the same oracle. This makes it possible for players to treat opponents simply as an ordinary part of this environment.

When an environment contains multiple agents playing a game against each other, the probabilistic behavior of the oracle may cause the players' behavior to be probabilistic as well. Reflective oracles are probabilistic computational constructs designed to answer queries about the output distributions of oracle machines—including those machines that themselves refer to the same oracle. This self-referential capability underlies a range of foundational results in game theory, decision theory, computability, effective topos theory, and synthetic mathematics. Reflective oracles avoid classical diagonalization obstacles by randomizing their responses on certain queries, enabling consistent solutions to paradoxical or self-referential prediction problems. This feature allows agents equipped with reflective oracle access to model their environment and other agents in an undistinguished manner, providing new decision-theoretic foundations for game-theoretic equilibrium and substantially broadening the scope of oracle-based reasoning.



The randomization in the tie case is essential, preventing the oracle from producing contradictions arising from self-referential queries (e.g., liar-type paradoxes found in naïve diagonalization arguments). This property guarantees existence of reflective oracles and supports robust reasoning in environments where agents and subsystems recursively consult the same probabilistic resource. Classical game theory assigns special status to players, explicitly enumerating them within the model. The reflective oracle paradigm removes this distinction: agents and the environment are uniformly treated as oracle machines with access to a shared reflective oracle (Fallenstein et al., 2015). In this configuration, mixed strategies in Nash equilibria naturally arise from the oracle's inherent randomization. Each agent evaluates the consequences of its actions by modeling both itself and its coplayers as oracle machines.

Furthermore, given any polynomial-time method for writing down computer programs that provably fail to halt, logical inductors learn to believe that they will fail to halt roughly as fast as the source codes can be generated. Coherence can be thought of as a generalization of the notion of "consistency" to probability distributions over sentences in logic. However, coherent distributions are uncomputable—they assign probability 1 to all theorems, and thus, they must assign probability 1 to the statement "computation f outputs x" whenever f() = x. For this reason, coherent probability distributions cannot represent a state of uncertainty about the outputs of computations. Rather, they represent a final state of knowledge about logical facts that a reasoner might obtain if they could think forever (Cozic 2006; Halpern and Pucella 2011).

Demski (2012) has proposed instead investigating algorithms that *computably approximate* a coherent probability distribution, that is, algorithms that output a series of probabilities for each sentence such that those probabilities converge in the limit, and such that the

distribution the approximation converges to is coherent. 

We say that coherence is a generalization of consistency because P agrees with T on all theorems and contradictions, but can assign probabilities to undecidable sentences so long as those probabilities obey logical constraints. Gaifman (1964) has shown that any coherent P is isomorphic to a measure  $\mu$  on complete consistent extensions of T—in other words, a coherent P assigns probability to undecidable sentences in a fashion that corresponds to choosing some weighted mixture of all possible consistent ways to assign truth values to sentences.

Coherence is a very strong constraint. For example, if T is PA, then P must assign probability 1 to all true statements about the behavior of computations. One way to think of a coherent distribution is that it represents the state of knowledge a reasoner could achieve after thinking forever, after proving everything provable, refuting everything refutable, and assigning consistent

In this paper, I argue that the problem of induction dissolves when recast in terms of logical coherence (understood as internal consistency of credences under updating) rather than truth. Following E. T. Jaynes, probability is interpreted not as frequency or decision rule but as the extension of deductive logic to incomplete information. Under this interpretation, Bayes's theorem is not an empirical statement but a consistency condition that constrains rational belief updating. Induction thus emerges as the special case of deductive reasoning applied to uncertain premises.

Falsification appears as the limiting form of Bayesian updating when new data drive posterior plausibility toward zero, while the Bayes Factor quantifies the continuous spectrum of evidential strength.



Hume The Skeptical Challenge: shows that no finite observation can justify universal inference; the uniformity of nature cannot be proven logically.
- 2. Laplace The Probabilistic Bridge: transforms Hume's puzzle into a quantitative problem, proposing probability as a measure of rational expectation, yet revealing *probability dilution*: even perfect evidence cannot confirm a universal law.
- 3. Jeffreys The Objective Prior: attempts to restore universality by assigning prior mass to immutable laws, solving the arithmetic but not the logic of induction.
- 4. Popper and Fisher The Procedural Turn: replace belief with decision; falsification and confidence provide rules for action, not coherent justification.
- 5. Jaynes The Logical Resolution: reframes probability as the *extension of logic* to *incomplete information*, unifying induction, falsification, and maximum entropy under the single principle of coherence.
Cournot's "forgotten" principle is one way of giving meaning to probabilistic statements like, "the relative frequency of heads of a fair coin converges to 1/2 with probability 1". The contraposition of Cournot is that one must assign non-zero probability to possible events. If "events" are described by sentences and "possible" means it is possible to satisfy these sentences, i.e. they possess a model, then we arrive at the strong Cournot principle that satisfiable sentences should be assigned non-zero probability (Definitions 25 and 35). This condition has been appropriately called 'non-dogmatic' in [GS82]. As long as something is not proven false, there is a (small) chance it is valid in the intended interpretation. This nondogmatism is crucial in Bayesian inductive reasoning, since no evidence (however strong) can increase a zero prior belief to a non-zero posterior belief [RH11].

Scott Garrabrant Tsvi Benson-Tilsen Andrew Critch Nate Soares Jessica Taylor
